4.1.1.6 Operational Multi-Crew Limitation (OML)  (A) The limitation “valid only as or with qualified co-pilot” is to be applied when the holder of a CPL or an ATPL(A) does not fully meet the class 1 medical certificate requirements and has been referred to the licensing authority, it shall be assessed whether the medical certificate may be issued with an OML "valid only as or with qualified co-pilot". This assessment shall be performed by the licensing authority. This limitation is applied in the context of a multi-pilot environment. The OML for Class 1 medical certificates may only be imposed and removed by the licensing authority. (B) Any flight crew composition which contains a member with an OML endorsement shall be composed so as to ensure that the remaining flight crew member(s): 1. has not attained the age of 60 years; 2. is not subject to an OML; 3. shall be fully qualified on the relevant type of aircraft; and 4. co-pilots shall log at least 300 hours flight time (simulator flight hours are not included) on the applicable aeroplane type according to Turkish DGCA Directive DK.22.112 OML Constitute Of Constrained Pilots And Air Crew. Note: Note the requirements above may be omitted for TRI/TRE Commanders who are issued OML endorsement after being delegated as TRI/TRE, while they are occupying observer’s seat for conducting check flights. Such TRI/TRE Commanders shall not be considered as a part of the augmented flight crew for the purposes of extending the flight duty period. (C) OML restricted pilots shall inform the appropriate Fleet Manager upon being issued an OML endorsement prior to accepting any flight duties for Turkish Airlines. It is the Fleet Managers’ responsibility to inform the required departments of the restrictions imposed. (D) It is the responsibility of each flight crew member to inform the remaining flight crew member(s) of any OML endorsement issued on the Class 1 Medical Certificate. (E) A Commander shall not be selected as CI or CN for a specific type of aeroplane if OML endorsement is issued. (F) If a Commander is issued an OML endorsement after being delegated as TRI or TRE, he may continue his duty with restrictions stated above unless a contrary decision is given by the Instructor Selection and Evaluation Board. (G) If a flight crew member has been issued an OML endorsement, this information shall be shared with the cabin crew members during the pre-flight briefing.  4.1.1.7 Crewing of Inexperienced Flight Crew Members  (A) Turkish Airlines established procedure (approved by the Turkish DGCA) prevents the crewing of inexperienced flight crew members together as described in   Subchapter 4.1.1.8 (B). (B) There shall not be more than one inexperienced flight crew member (inexperienced crew shall be classified as restricted crew) at controls. However, when at least one C1 or higher classified Commander is on board and, C2 and P5 (restricted crew members) are part of additional flight crew member composition; C2 Commander should not be considered as inexperienced provided that, following completion of a type rating or command course, and the associated line flying under supervision, if he has achieved on the type either: 1. 100 flight hours and flown 10 sectors within a consolidation period of 120 consecutive days; or 2. 150 flight hours and flown 20 sectors (no time limit). It shall be assured that the flight from block-off until FL200 and from FL200 down to block-on in confirmation with the requirements of  Subchapter 4.1.1.8 (B) as per item (E). (C)   Respective   Fleet   Management   and/or   Flight   Operations   Support   Management   and   the   respective   flight   crew   member   are responsible for tracking and maintaining accurate records of the required flying hours and sectors during the period when a pilot is classified as “Restricted”. (D) Upon completion of the required flight hours, the “Restricted” classification of a pilot may only be lifted by the Senior Vice President, Flight Operations (Chief Pilot), after review of all relevant pending documents (ground training, simulator training, LIFUS) at the recommendation of the Fleet Manager. (E) It is the responsibility of the designated Commander to ensure that all flight crew members conduct the flight from block-off until FL200 and from FL200 down to block-on in confirmation with the requirements of   Subchapter 4.1.1.8 (B). C2   Commander “RESTRICTED”  (A)   Commanders   shall   be   classified   as   restricted   until   the   following requirements are met; 1. at least 300 accumulated flight hours (200 hours for Commanders joining another Turkish Airlines Fleet) within 12 calendar months; and 2. once the required 300 flight hours is completed, the relevant Fleet Manager shall   evaluate   and,   may   recommend   the   Commander   for   an   upgrade. (B) Commanders who meet the requirements of above items will be subject to a classification assessment for an upgrade to C1 status. If the Commander is not recommended after the assessment, he will be rescheduled for a new classification assessment after accumulating at least another 300 flight hours. Once the required flight hours are completed, the relevant Fleet Manager shall evaluate   and,   may   again   recommend   the   Commander   for   C1   upgrade. However, this recommendation shall be made not later than 12 calendar months of the previous classification assessment. 4.1.2.7 Supernumeraries  (A) A supernumerary is a person in addition to the flight crew that is not a cabin crew member, but is on board either a cargo or passenger aircraft during commercial or non-commercial operations, and is not classified as a passenger by the operator or the Authority. Such person is typically any of the following: 1. Assigned to the flight by the operator as necessary for the safety of operations and has certain (operator required) knowledge and abilities gained through selection and mandatory training (e.g. loadmaster, animal handler, dangerous goods handler, cargo attendant, security guard, etc.). 2. An inspector, auditor or observer authorized by the operator and the State to be on board the aircraft in the performance of his or her duties (e.g. DGCA flight operations inspector, IOSA auditor, LOSA observer, etc.) 3. Assigned to a passenger flight by the operator to conduct certain customer service activities (e.g. serving beverages, conducting customer relations, selling tickets, flying chefs, flying service chefs, Vocational Education Students (Cabin), translators, etc.) in the cabin; not designated to perform any safety duties. 4. Any other individual that has a relationship with the operator, is not classified as a passenger by the Authority and authorized by the operator and the State to be on board the aircraft (e.g., courier, escorts, technical staff, contract coordinator, individual with operator- required knowledge and abilities traveling to/from a duty assignment, company employee or dependent in the supernumerary compartment of a cargo aircraft). (B) Supernumeraries shall not wear a uniform in passenger flights which might identify them to the passengers as being a cabin crew member unless they are qualified as a cabin crew member. (C) Supernumeraries shall not be given any duty that is related to safety unless their duties and responsibilities are defined and they are trained, evaluated and certified in the performance of any assigned duties or functions. (D) Supernumeraries shall not impede, neither flight crew nor cabin crew members, in the performance of their duties. (E) Refer to   EK.10.73.003 Operations Manual Part-B A330/350 Chapter 14.3.1. Occupants of Cargo Aircraftand EK.10.73.004  Operations Manual Part-B Boeing 777/787 Chapter 14.3.1 Occupants of Cargo Aircraft for the maximum number of supernumeraries to be carried on board at cargo flights. (F) See EK.10.71.001 Cabin Crew Manual Chapter 4.7. Principles of Presence of Employee in Cabin other than Assigned Cabin Crew.  4.1.3. Common Language  (A) Use of common language shall be ensured by all crew members: 1. On the flight crew compartment during line operations, 2. Between the flight crew and cabin crew during line operations, 3. During flight crew training and evaluation activities. (B) In addition, effective communication shall be established and maintained between flight crew members and cabin crew members: 1. During normal, abnormal and emergency operations, 2. In the event of incapacitation of any crew member.  (C)   Crew composition shall ensure that all allocated crew members can communicate in a common language: Between flight crew members   Turkish and/or English. Between flight crew members (Flight Crew/non–Turkish   English. Between cabin crew members   Turkish and/or English. Between crew members   Turkish and/or English. Designation of the Commander  (A) One Commander amongst the flight crew, qualified to operate as pilot-in-command will be assigned as the designated Commander for a particular flight by the Crew Planning Directorate (in accordance with EASA Regulations, Turkish DGCA Regulations and requirements specified within this chapter). (B) The designated Commander shall meet the qualification requirements, including knowledge of the route or area to be flown and of the aerodromes, including alternate aerodromes, facilities and procedures to be used and other requirements such as low visibility, age, OML, CRM, recency and other qualification requirements specified within   Chapter 4,   Chapter 5 and   EK.10.72.001 Operations Manual Part-D Chapter 2.1. Flight Crew. (C) The Commander or the pilot, to whom the conduct of the flight may be delegated, shall have had initial familiarization training of the route or area to be flown and of the aerodromes, facilities and procedures to be used. This route/area and aerodrome knowledge shall be maintained by following: 1. operating at least once to the aerodrome within a 12-month period. 2. The route or area knowledge shall be maintained by operating at least once to the route or area within a 36 months’ period. In addition, refresher training is required regarding route or area knowledge if not operating on a route or area for 12 months within the 36-month period. 3. For details about compliance with this requirement for Category C aerodromes and the definition of the 12-month period, refer to  Subchapter 5.1.3.1.3. (D) The name of the senior Commander as designated Commander should appear on the Operational Flight Plan (OFP) as long as route, area and aerodrome competence qualification or recency/recent experience requirements are satisfied. The SFP and/or OFP or soft copy of OFP in the Electronic Flight Folder (EFF) module of the EFB shall be signed-off by the designated Commander. Any changes in designation of the Commander shall instantly be noted on the SFP/OFP in writing or if time permits, a new OFP may be issued. (E) When C2 and any higher classified commander are crewed together, the other CI, CN or C1 commander will always be designated commander regardless of seniority. (F) The assigned designated Commander will decide the Commander who will be occupying the left-hand seat during take-off and landing (except as described in item (I) (3) below for checks from C3 to C2 status). (G) The Commander or the cruise pilot occupying the left-hand seat during any phase of the flight has the responsibility for ensuring safe conduct of flight, which was delegated to them by the designated Commander. Any Turkish Airlines non-operating type qualified Commander on board (shall be competent for duty), Note: Note  Note 1 : Incapacitated flight crew member shall be unseated to make room for the qualified Commander. 3. QUALIFICATION REQUIREMENTS  5.1 License, Qualification, Training and Checking Requirements for Flight Crew 5.1.1 License Requirements  (A) To operate any Turkish Airlines aeroplane, a flight crew member shall possess the following: 1. a valid pilot licence (ATPL(A) or CPL(A)/IR, as applicable) with a respective type rating; including minimum of Level 4 ICAO language proficiency as applicable. 2. a valid Authorization Certificate (EASA licence) or Validation Certificate (ICAO licence) issued by Turkish DGCA, if applicable. 3. a valid Class 1 medical certificate (not to be valid for a period greater than 12 months). (B) All flight crew members are responsible for ensuring the validity of their licenses, certificates and ratings prior to accepting and/or conducting assigned flight duties with Turkish Airlines.  5.1.2 Ratings 5.1.2.1 Instrument Rating  (A) A pilot shall not act as pilot of a Turkish Airlines aeroplane under instrument flight rules (IFR) unless he has an instrument rating (IR). (B) An IR is valid for one year. If an IR is to be re-validated the holder shall complete a proficiency check within the three months immediately preceding the expiry date of the rating and the revalidation of an IR shall be combined with the type rating revalidation.  5.1.2.2 Type Rating  (A) The holder of a pilot licence shall not act as a pilot of a Turkish Airlines aeroplane unless he has a valid and appropriate type rating. 5.1.3.1.2. Aerodrome Knowledge  (A) The Commander or the pilot, to whom the conduct of the flight may be delegated, shall obtain adequate knowledge of destination and alternate aerodromes. Aerodrome competence qualification includes knowledge of obstructions, physical layout, lighting, approach aids and arrival, departure, holding and instrument approach procedures, applicable operating minima, Air Traffic Services (ATS) provided and ground movement considerations. ( EK.10.73.002 Operations Manual Part-C Jeppesen Airway Manual consisting of en- route charts, terminal charts and explanatory material shall be used as pictorial presentation). (B) All aerodromes to which Turkish Airlines operates are categorized in one of these three categories: 1. Category A: An aerodrome that meets all of the following requirements: a. a straight-in 3D instrument approach procedure with a glide path angle of not more than 3.5 degrees to each runway expected to be used for landing; b. at least one runway with no performance limited procedure for take-off and/or landing, such as no requirement to follow a contingency procedure for obstacle clearance in the event of an engine failure on take-off from any runway expected to be used for departure; and c. night operations capability. 2. Category B: An aerodrome that does not meet the category A requirements or which requires extra considerations due to: a. non-standard approach aids and/or approach patterns, such as restrictions on the availability of straight-in instrument approach procedures; b. unusual local weather conditions, such as environmental features that can give rise to turbulence, windshear or unusual wind conditions; c. unusual characteristics or performance limitations, such as unusual runway characteristics in length, width, slope, markings or lighting that present an atypical visual perspective on approach; d. any other relevant considerations, including obstructions, physical layout, lighting, etc., such as restrictions on circling in certain sectors due to obstacles in the circling area; e. training or flight crew experience requirements stipulated by the competent authority responsible for the aerodrome that do not include instruction in an FSTD or visiting the aerodrome. 3. Category C: An aerodrome that requires additional considerations to a category B aerodrome or for which flight crew experience or qualification requirements stipulated by the competent authority responsible for the aerodrome include instruction in an FSTD or visiting the aerodrome. (C) Prior to operating to/from a: 1. Category B aerodrome, each flight crew member shall be briefed, or self-briefed ( EK.10.73.002 Operations Manual Part-C Jeppesen Airway Manual including CCI pages and Aerodrome Information Note), by means of programmed instructions, on the Category B aerodrome(s) concerned. The completion of the briefing is recorded when Commander signs the SFP or electronically signs the OFP in Electronic Flight Folder (EFF) of the EFB, certifying that he has obtained adequate knowledge of aerodromes and comply with any requirements stipulated by the competent authority responsible for the aerodrome. This recording may be accomplished after completion or confirmed by the Commander on a flight involving category B aerodrome(s) as destination or alternate aerodromes. (C) The Commander (other than CN/CI) on the right-hand seat shall be PM all the time during approach, landing and take-off phases of flight except in abnormal situations.  5.1.3.4 Crew Resource Management Qualification  (A) All flight crew members shall complete an initial Crew Resource Management (CRM) training course before commencing unsupervised line flying. (B) Elements of CRM training shall be included in the aeroplane type rating training and recurrent training as well as in the command course. (C) See   EK.10.72.001 Operations Manual Part-D Chapter 2.1.1. Crew Resource Management (CRM) Course for further details about CRM Courses.  5.1.3.4.1 Crew Resource Management  (A) Crew resource management is the application of team management concepts and the effective use of all available resources to maximize flight safety by managing operational threats and human error. (B) These resources include, of but are not limited to; 1. Crewmember: Flight crew, cabin crew, dispatcher, 2. Resource: a. Liveware: ATC, dispatcher, maintenance, flight and ground operation personnel, load master, etc., b. Hardware: TCAS, Flaps/Slats, EGPWS, WX Radar, Altimeter etc., c. Software: FMS, ECAM, procedures and policies, d. Planning Resources: OFP, enroute chart, SIGMET, NOTAM, CSPD, etc., 3. Management: Leading, controlling, coordinating, cooperating, conflict solving. (C) Overall, incidents and accidents involve the entire range of CRM and human factors aspects. (D) CRM concepts and techniques enhance effective monitoring, crosschecking and backup by each crewmember.  5.1.3.4.1.1 Company Culture and Policies  Company safety culture and policies should: 1. Support the implementation of CRM practices; 2. Facilitate the mitigation of organizational factors; and, 3. Identify and address precursors of potential incidents or accidents.  5.1.3.4.1.2 International Cultural Factors  Cross-cultural factors should include: 1. Importance of cultural and national sensitivities; and, 2. Promoting the use of standard phraseology as a common working language.  5.1.3.4.1.3 Leadership  (A) The commander must demonstrate the focus and energy required to motivate the crewmembers to work together as a team. (B) The role of the commander in complex and demanding situations should be emphasized during CRM training.  5.1.3.4.1.4 Teamwork  (A) Effective teamwork requires effective command and leadership by the commander and effective support by all crewmembers. (B) Teamwork enhances the crew problem-solving capability in dealing with normal and non-normal situations. (C) Achieving effective teamwork requires the optimum use of the following crew resources: 1. Communication skills; 2. Monitoring skills; 3. Technical proficiency; 4. Advocacy/inquiry; and, 5. Dedication to success. (D) Performing a pre-flight briefing that includes the flight crew and cabin crew establishes the basis for effective teamwork.  5.1.3.4.1.5 Situational Awareness  (A) Situational Awareness is: 1. The perception of the elements in the environment within a volume of time and space, 2. The comprehension of their meaning, 3. The projection of their status in the near future. (B) The main components of situational awareness are: 1. Environmental Awareness (awareness of other aircraft, communications between ATC and other aircraft, weather or terrain). 2. Mode Awareness (awareness of aircraft configuration and auto flight system modes). 3. Spatial Orientation (awareness of geographical position and aircraft attitude). 4. System Awareness (awareness of status of aircraft systems). 5. Time Horizon - time management (e.g., fuel status/monitoring, time factor in smoke situation or nonnormal electrical configuration). (C) Situational awareness is having an accurate understanding of what is happening around you and what is likely to happen in the near future. (D) Situational awareness influences our decision-making and allows us to stay ahead of the aircraft: (E) Situational awareness is essential for flight safety and its influence and impact are pervasive. (F) Situational awareness is gained by using the senses to scan the environment and compare the results with mental models. (G) Planning, communication and coordination for up-coming flight phases, goal setting and feedback are essential ingredients of situational awareness and decision making. (H) Inattention, distraction and high workload threatens situational awareness. (I) To prevent the loss of situational awareness: 1. Adhere to standardized procedures, sterile flight deck rules, standard calls, CRM, instrument scan, etc. 2. Strictly follow company operation manuals.  5.1.3.4.1.6 Assertiveness  (A) Incidents and accidents illustrate that if an option (e.g., performing a go-around) has not been prepared, flight crew members may lack the mental resources needed to: 1. Make the required decision (i.e., initiate the go-around); or, 2. Correctly conduct the required maneuver (i.e., flying the published missed approach). (B) Fatigue or reluctance to change a prepared plan often is the probable causes for a lack of assertiveness (assessment of situation) and decision making. 5.1.3.4.1.7 Time Management  Developing multi-tasking ability and ensuring task prioritization are essential factors in staying ahead of the aircraft; beware of tasks that are time consuming.  5.1.3.4.1.8 Threat Management  (A) A threat is a condition that affects or complicates the performance of a task or the compliance with applicable standards. (B) The analysis of the operational and human factors when performing operational events, should consist the following aspects; 1. Threat anticipated and briefed; 2. Threat avoided/prevented; 3. Threat not recognized; 4. Threat consequential or inconsequential; 5. Threat managed/recovered/mitigated; and/or, 6. Late identification of threat, assessment and management.  5.1.3.4.1.9 Error Management  (A) Flight crew errors often are induced by interruptions and distractions resulting from: 1. Intra-flight deck activities; or, 2. External threats (e.g., ATC instructions, weather conditions, etc.) (B) The most critical aspect in discussing error management is not the initial error or deviation but the failure to detect this error or deviation, by mutual monitoring and backup. (C) The analysis of the operational and human factors when performing operational events, should consist of the following aspects; 1. Detected or undetected inadvertent action; 2. Detected or undetected action slip; 3. Detected or undetected entry error; 4. Detected error challenged or not; 5. Detected error corrected or not; 6. Error outcome consequential or inconsequential; 7. Error resulting or not in an aircraft undesired state; and, 8. Successful or unsuccessful recovery technique/action.  5.1.3.4.1.10 Risk Management  (A) The concept of risk combines the notions of severity and probability, with reference to a given hazard. (B) A hazard is a condition that has the potential to cause personal injury or death, property damage or operational degradation. (C) The severity of a given threat rarely can be significantly reduced but its probability of occurrence can be largely reduced by implementing related prevention strategies (e.g., safety awareness and training programs). (D) For the flight crewmembers, risk management often consists in assessing the effects of potential hazards on the safe conduct of the flight and in finding ways to avoid these hazards or to minimize their effects. (E) Decision making is to be considered as risk management at flight crew members level. (F) Risk management also should be seen as a balanced management of priorities. 5.1.3.4.1.11 Resource Management  Standards for CRM shall be constituted with: (A) Briefings that are interactive and emphasize the importance of questions, critique, and the offering of information. (B) Encouragement of crew members to speak up and state their information with appropriate persistence until there is a clear resolution. (C) Acceptance of criticism objectively and non-defensively. (D) Recognition of the effects of stress and fatigue on performance. (E) Friendly, relaxed and supportive tone of flight deck. (F) Crew members adapting to other members personalities. (G) Crew members acting decisively when required. (H) Inclusion of crew members as part of a team in briefings, as appropriate, and guidelines are established for coordination between flight deck and cabin. (I) Avoidance of complacency. (J) Clear communication of decisions about the operation of flight. (K) Involving the entire crewmembers in the decision-making process. (L) Encouragement of individuals to offer ideas. (M) Clear, accurate statement of information about problems that shall be provided with an appropriate degree of urgency.  5.1.3.4.1.12 Decision Making  (A) Effective flight crew decision making requires a joint evaluation of possible options prior to proceeding with an agreed decision and action. (B) This process includes defining the problem, generating possible solutions, risk assessment and the time available. (C) A decision-making model for time critical situations often is an effective technique to lessen the effects of pressure caused by the dynamics of the situation. (D) Decision making model should share the following phases: 1. Recognizing the prevailing condition (i.e., identifying the problem); 2. Assessing   short   term   and   long-term   consequences   on   the   flight   (i.e.,   collecting   the   facts   and   assessing   their   operational implications); 3. Evaluating available options and procedures (i.e., identifying and evaluating alternatives); 4. Deciding the course of actions (i.e., selecting the best mutually-agreed alternative); 5. Taking actions in accordance with the defined procedures and applicable task sharing (i.e., implementing the selected option); 6. Evaluating and monitoring action results (i.e., confirming expectations versus observed facts); and, 7. Resuming standard flying duties (i.e., resuming operation in accordance with SOP’s, including the use of standard calls and normal checklists). (E) The above decision-making model should optimize the available crew resources in terms of: 1. Interpersonal communications; 2. Inquiry and advocacy; 3. Effective listening; 4. Tasks prioritization ability; E K . 1 0 . 7 3 . 0 0 1 | R e v i s i o n 0 6 O p e r a t i o n s M a n u a l P a r t - A QMS Document Template Number: FR.18.0001 | Revision 12 Document Template Reference Document Number: TL.18.006 Page: 113 | Total Page: 466 Copy of this document has been generated on 9.01.2026 21:53. Controlled and legally valid originals of all documents can be accessed from the DDMS located at ddms.thy.com. All printed and electronic copies outside of the DDMS are uncontrolled copies.

5. Self-confidence, but also self-critical-analysis. (F) Postponing a decision until that option is no more considered or no longer available is a recurring pattern in incidents and accidents, particularly in approach and landing accidents. (G) The concepts of next-target and approach-gate are intended to act as milestones for supporting a timely decisionmaking process.  5.1.3.4.1.13 Other CRM Aspects  The following other CRM aspects have been observed in most incidents or accidents: (A) Spatial disorientation (i.e., physiological illusions and/or visual illusions); (B) Complacency when operating at a familiar aerodrome (e.g., home base); or, (C) Overconfidence; (D) Inadequate anticipation (i.e., inability to stay ahead of the aircraft); (E) Inadequate preparation to respond to changing situations or to a non-normal condition, by precise planning and use of all available technical and human resources (i.e., by expecting the unexpected); (F) Crew members personal factors; and/or, (G) Absence of specific training of instructors and check airmen to evaluate the CRM performance of trainees and line pilots.  5.1.3.4.1.14 Factors Affecting CRM Practice  The following organizational or personal factors may adversely affect the effective implementation of CRM practices: (A) Company culture and policies, (B) Belief that actions or decisions are correct, although they may deviate from the applicable standards, (C) Effect of fatigue and absence of countermeasures to restore the level of vigilance and alertness, (D) Reluctance to accept the influence of human factors and CRM issues in incidents or accidents.  5.1.3.4.1.15 Summary of Key Points  (A) CRM practices optimize the performance of the entire crew (i.e., including cabin crewmembers and maintenance personnel). (B) CRM skills effectively; 1. Relieve the effects of pressures, interruptions and distractions; 2. Provide milestones for timely decision making; and, 3. Provide safeguards for effective error management, thus minimizing the effects of working errors.  5.1.3.5 Other Qualifications for Flight Crew  (A) Flight crew members, where applicable, shall possess following qualifications depending on the requirements of the route they fly and/or type of operation they are involved in: 1. CREW HEALTH PRECAUTIONS  6.1 Crew Health Precautions 6.1.1 General  (A) Crew health is of the highest importance and has a direct impact on flight safety. A crew member shall not perform duties on an aeroplane at any time when he is aware of any decrease in his medical fitness which might render him unable to safely exercise his duties. (B) Licence holders shall not exercise the privileges of their licence and related ratings or certificates, at any time when they: 1. are aware of any decrease in their medical fitness which might render them unable to safely exercise those privileges; 2. take or use any prescribed or non-prescribed medication which is likely to interfere with the safe exercise of the privileges of the applicable licence; 3. receive any medical, surgical or other treatment that is likely to interfere with the safe exercise of the privileges of the applicable licence. (C) In addition, holders of a medical certificate shall, without undue delay and before exercising the privileges of their licence, shall consult to Human Resources Directorate/Asst.Dir.Human Resources (Health) Department for the circumstances stated below to seek aero-medical advice as applicable, when they: 1. have undergone a surgical operation or invasive procedure; 2. have commenced the regular use of any medication; 3. have suffered any significant personal injury involving incapacity to function as a member of the flight crew; 4. have been suffering from any significant illness involving incapacity to function as a member of the flight crew; 5. are pregnant; 6. have been admitted to hospital or medical clinic; 7. first require correcting lenses. In that case, the AME, AeMC or OHMP shall assess the medical fitness of the cabin crew members and decide whether they are fit to resume their safety duties. The authority will be informed regarding the injury, pregnancy or illness. The medical certificate shall be deemed to be suspended upon the occurrence of such injury or the elapsed period of illness or the confirmation of pregnancy until the medical state of the medical certificate owner is evaluated and agreed to gain medical privileges of the medical certificate. For detailed information, see PR.10.30.038 Procedure for Aviation Medicine Practices Section 6.5. Aviation Examination Processes for Determination of Cockpit and Cabin Crew Members’ Fitness for Flight in case of Decrease in Medical Fitness. Psychoactive Substances (PS) Related Matters  (A) The use of Psychoactive Substances (PS) by flight crew members is prohibited by the Turkish DGCA. (B) If a flight crew member is suspected to be under the influence of any PS prior to flight, the other flight crew member shall immediately inform Flight Operations Directorate and ensure the required actions are taken. (C)   PR.10.35.097 Procedure For Medical Examination For Alcohol And Psychoactive Substances Section 6.2. (F) Consumption of poppy seeds and meals containing these seeds are prohibited since reliability of the psychoactive substance tests are affected. 6.1.3 Alcohol and Other Intoxicating Liquor  (A) A crew member shall not consume alcohol during the flight duty period or whilst on standby duty. (B) A crew member shall not consume or continue to consume alcohol at least 12 hours prior to the specified reporting time for a flight duty, or the commencement of standby duty. (C) If the crew member is on a lay-over, consumption of alcohol shall be ended at least 12 hours prior to the time he is available for a duty after his legal resting time is over (due to the fact that he might be called for a duty any time). (D) In case of being on a reserve duty, the crew member shall stop consuming alcohol as of 11:59 am LT previous day. (E) Since the metabolism of alcohol in the blood is very slow, it is highly recommended that crew members refrain from the consumption of alcohol 24 hours before the expected commencement of flight duty or standby. (F) The max blood alcohol level, which allows a commencement of a duty, is 0.2 promile. (G) As a company policy, crew members on duty or in uniform (e.g., after termination of flight duty; deadheading crew members) shall not consume alcoholic beverages where they can be observed by third parties, i.e., the public. (H) To the general public all crew members shall convey a non-drinking image. During layovers, the crew members should refrain from frequenting places if there is the possibility that this image might be compromised. The crew members shall also ensure that other crew members comply with this regulation. (I) During layovers, crew members whom are appointed by Turkish Airlines, starting from the end of a flight duty until the beginning of a new one, shall arrange their behaviors according to Company policies and ethical values, national and international laws, general moral values and when present special local values including cultural differences of the place of accommodation and they shall be aware that they are representing Turkish Airlines during the period between two flight duties. (J) Any crew member violating the alcohol regulations shall expect severe disciplinary measures, in extreme cases leading to immediate discharge from the company. (K) The Authority reminds crew members that the excessive use of alcohol may result in withdrawal of the crew member’s license and privileges.  6.1.4 Narcotics  (A) The term ‘narcotics’ covers heroin, morphine, cocaine, cannabis, amphetamines and other stimulants. (B) For crew members, the consumption or use of narcotics is strictly prohibited.  6.1.5 Drugs  (A) Drug is the general name for any substance (prescribed medication, over-the-counter medication, drugs, selfmedication etc.) that has an influence on the mental or physical health of a crew member. (B) A crew member shall not perform any duties on an aeroplane while under the influence of any drug that may affect his abilities in a manner contrary to safety. (C) Any crew member using drugs containing alcohol derivatives or psychoactive drugs (specified in   LS.35.024 List Of Drugs Affecting  Flight Safety ) because of his illness, is obliged to report his status to the Company together with medical certificate and prescription. (D) Antibiotics such as various Penicillin, Tetracycline and others may have short term or delayed side effects, which can affect pilot performance. More significantly, their use usually indicates that an infection is present and thus the effects of this infection will normally mean that a pilot is not fit to fly. A pilot should have previous experience of the antibiotic prescribed, or, alternatively, have a trial of it for at least twenty-four hours on the ground before using it during his flight duties. (E) Inability to react due to the use of tranquillizers, anti-depressants and sedatives has been a contributory cause to fatal aircraft accidents. Flight duties should not be resumed until treatment with these types of drugs has been discontinued and until the effects of the drugs have entirely worn off. This can take several days in some instances. (F) Stimulants such as caffeine, amphetamine etc. (often known as ‘’pep-pills’’) used to maintain wakefulness or suppress appetite are often habit forming. Susceptibility to different stimulants varies from one individual to another, and all may cause dangerous levels of over confidence. Over dosage causes headaches, dizziness and mental disturbance. The use of “pep-pills” while flying is not permitted. Remember that excessive coffee drinking has harmful effects including disturbance of the heart rhythm. (G) Anti-histamines can cause drowsiness. They are widely used in ‘’cold-cures’’ and in treatment of hay fever, asthma and allergic rashes. They may be in tablet form or a constituent of nasal drops or sprays. In many cases the condition itself may preclude flying. If treatment is necessary, crew member shall consult Human Resources Directorate/Asst.Dir.Human Resources (Health) department or Turkish Airlines Airport Apron Health Department, so that modern drugs, which do not degrade human performance, can be prescribed. (H) Certain drugs used to treat high blood pressure can cause a change in the normal cardiovascular reflexes and impair intellectual performance, both of which can seriously affect flight safety. If the level of blood pressure is such that drug therapy is required, the pilot must   be   temporarily   grounded   and   monitored   for   any   side   effects.   Any   treatment   shall   be   consulted   to   Human   Resources Directorate/Asst.Dir.Human Resources (Health) department.  6.1.6 Sleeping Tablets  (A) Sleeping tablets can dull the senses, cause mental confusion and slow reactions. The length of time they act on any one individual varies, but may be prolonged, and crew members must have expert advice before using them. Some short acting medication with the approval of Human Resources Directorate/Asst.Dir.Human Resources (Health) department is acceptable in certain circumstances. (B) To prevent any undesirable or unexpected individual reaction, the particular medication must first be tried before on a rest day and shall not be consumed on duty.  6.1.7 Pharmaceutical Preparations  (A) Many preparations are now marketed containing a combination of medicines. If there is any change in the medication or dosage, the effect should be observed by the crew member on the ground, prior to flying duties. Although the above explained are the most common medicines which adversely affect pilot performance, it should be noted that many other forms of medications, although not normally affecting pilot performance, many do so in individuals who are ‘’oversensitive’’ to a particular preparation. Individuals are therefore   advised   not   to   take   any   medication   before   or   during   flight   unless   they   consult   to   Human   Resources Directorate/Asst.Dir.Human Resources (Health) department . (B) If you are ill and need treatment, it is vitally important that the doctor to whom you consult knows that you are a flight crew member and crew member shall always consult to Human Resources Directorate/Asst.Dir.Human Resources (Health) department when a treatment is required. For detailed information, see PR.10.30.038 Procedure for Aviation Medicine Practices Section 6. Implementation. (C) Other alternative or complementary treatments, such as acupuncture, homoeopathy, hypnotherapy and several other disciplines, is developing and gaining greater credibility. Some such treatments are more acceptable in some states than others. There is a need to ensure that ‘’other treatments ‘’, as well as the underlying condition, are declared and considered by the Human Resources Directorate/Asst.Dir.Human Resources (Health) department when assessing fitness to fly.  6.1.8 Immunization / Vaccination  (A) It is essential for all airline staff that travel to be protected against the common endemic diseases by immunization and malaria prophylaxis as appropriate. Vaccination is the most efficient means of prophylaxis for a number of infectious diseases. Vaccination is also generally effective and well tolerated. (B) Crew members and other personnel attending flights operated to territories where Yellow Fever vaccination is mandatory and any country which requires International Vaccination Certificate for entry shall be administered with Yellow Fever vaccines. The operating procedure is described in PR.35.451 Vaccination Practices Procedure Section 6. Implementation. (C) Flight crew members shall carry their vaccination records and ensure that they are kept current. Health Authorities at many airports may demand to inspect these documents and difficulties can arise if crew vaccination records are found to be invalid. (D) Each crew member scheduled for flight duty abroad must satisfy any requirement(s) for vaccination(s), to have himself vaccinated in time, and to be able to produce – during his tour of duty – the appropriate WHO – approved ‘’Certificate of Vaccination or Revaccination’’. (E) Pilots are advised not to fly within 24 hours after receiving an old preparation of vaccine, but new preparations have no side effect, therefore no delay is required. (F) In case of strong reaction, medical advice shall be obtained in view of a possible impairment of fitness for flight duty. No alcoholic beverages shall be consumed for a period of at least 24 hours after vaccination. (G) Crew members scheduled for flight duty to malaria-infected countries shall keep FR.35.0858 Malaria Information Card with them. It is necessary to apply to Istanbul Airport Turkish Airlines Apron Health Department to acquire information about the disease and the country to be visited and fly-repellent spray no later than one or two days before flying to the regions included in LS.35.042 List of Countries with Malaria Risk. For detailed information, see PR.10.35.096 Procedure for Malaria Protection and Control Measures Section 6.4. Rules to be observed by Employees to visit Risky Regions. 6.1.10 Blood/Plasma/Bone Marrow Donation  Flight crew members normally should not act as blood donors. If for any reason they have done so, they are to advise the company immediately following each donation, and shall not undertake flying duties for at least 24 hours after they have given blood/plasma/bone marrow. Flight crew members shall report to an AME for hemoglobin determination and blood count prior to an assigned flight duty.  6.1.11. Meal Precautions Prior to and During Flight  (A) In the interest of safety, crew members shall not consume identical/same dishes prepared by the same caterer, restaurant or person before or during a flight. (B) Since the most acute forms of food poisoning frequently occur 1-6 hours after contaminated food is eaten, the crew member should exercise utmost care in respect of meals taken within 6 hours of a flight. For any crew member, before and during flight, it is essential to avoid eating easily perishable foods as well as foods and drinks served cold. This is most important with milk and cream products, mayonnaise sauces, salads, meat pies and other meat products. (C) The character and severity of the symptoms depend on the nature and dose of the toxin and the resistance of the patient. Onset may be sudden. Malaise anorexia, nausea, vomiting abdominal cramps, intestinal gurgling, diarrhea and varying degree of prostration may be experienced. Bed rest with convenient access to bathroom commode or bedpan is desirable. Severe cases should be hospitalized. Treatment is mostly symptomatic and all cases should be inspected by a doctor. (D) In-flight, crew meals should be served at their workstation, but the following shall be considered: 1. meals shall not be served to both flight crew members at the same time, 2. spilling food or beverages anywhere in the flight deck shall be avoided. If significant spillage occurred, an entry in the AML shall be made, and 3. for safety reasons no open drinks, glasses or glass bottles, porcelains shall be present in the flight deck during the phase of take-off and landing. (E) Meals which are to be served to crew members shall not contain poppy seeds as their consumption is prohibited.  6.1.12 Sleep and Rest  (A) Like food and water, sleep is a physiological need, vital to human survival and critical to human existence. Sleep loss can be additive and will result in a cumulative sleep debt, together with a feeling of increased waking sleepiness. The sleep debt must be repaid, and the symptoms of sleepiness shall be taken seriously in view of their profound effects on waking performance, mood and alertness. (B) Flight safety requires that all crewmembers receive regular and sufficient sleep and are well rested when commencing flight duty. Legal provisions (refer to   Chapter 7) therefore prescribe maximum duty and minimum rest times. The most successful technique for combating sleepiness in the operational environment is physical activity. Therefore, whenever possible, crew members should engage in an activity that involves physical action, even if it is only stretching. When appropriate, they should engage in conversations with others and ensure they participate and do not just nod and listen. (C) A crew member shall not perform duties on an aeroplane if he knows or suspects that he is suffering from fatigue, or feels unfit to the extent that the flight may be endangered. Note: Note For controlled rest on the flight deck, refer to   Subchapter 8.3.  6.1.13 Surgical Operations  Crew members shall consult to Human Resources Directorate/ Asst.Dir.Human Resources (Health) Department. When medical fitness is assured after the surgery a fitness certificate signed by an AME shall be produced prior to returning to flying duties otherwise he will be referred for further medical evaluation.  6.1.14 Administration of Anesthesia  Every holder of a medical certificate shall inform the Company Aviation Medical Examiners Supervisor's Office if he needs to get anesthesia. Flight Duty Practices for Pregnant Cockpit/Cabin Crew Members. (A) Pregnancy is a normal physiological process; however, major anatomical and hormonal disturbances are associated with it, which increase the risk of incapacitation accordingly. (B) Thirty to forty percent of pregnant women bleed or have cramping pains some time during the first twenty weeks of pregnancy. Twenty percent spontaneously abort; the majority of these take place within the first trimester. (C) It is important that the supervising physician can confirm pregnancy and apparent normality before the pilot continues flying. (D) The crew members are obliged to inform the Human Resources Directorate/Asst.Dir.Human Resources (Health) department about their pregnancy. The Health Department will refer the pregnant crew member to the AMS. The AMS shall provide written advice to the applicant and the supervising physician regarding potentially significant complications of pregnancy. Continuous antenatal care is vital to the early detection of abnormalities and so monthly assessments are required to maintain certification up to twenty-six weeks. (E) Beyond this point the incidence of gastro-intestinal disturbance associated with hormonal and anatomical displacement is such that even multi-pilot (Class 1 ‘OML’) or LIFUS Observer Pilot (Class 2 ‘OSL’) operation may be compromised, and so a temporarily unfit assessment is appropriate. (F) The AMS may approve certification of pregnant air crew for multi-pilot (Class 1 ‘OML’), single-pilot (Class 2) operations during the first 26 weeks of gestation following review of the obstetric evaluation. Monthly obstetric reports are required. (G) The pregnant pilot must also consider the cumulative effects of pressure changes and radiation exposure upon the developing fetus, although these are not of immediate flight safety concern. (H) Following confinement or termination of pregnancy, the individual may be considered for recertification after examination has been carried out to confirm involution has taken place (normally four to six weeks after confinement or termination).  6.1.16 Vision Correction  (A) All flight crew members that are required by the AME to wear corrective lenses in order to satisfy visual requirements laid down for granting of licenses, are required to carry a spare pair of spectacles, easily accessible to them on all occasions whilst operating with their license. Spectacles, either corrective or antiglare, when worn by flight crew during flight, should be of a type of frame that allows maximum peripheral vision. The examination for the prescription of a spectacle correction should ideally be carried out by an examiner with some understanding of the problems of vision in aviation. (B) Where the only correction necessary is for reading, pilots should never use full lens spectacles while flying because the pilot’s task requires frequent changes from near to distant vision and the latter is blurred by reading glasses. Halfmoon spectacles or lower segment lenses with a neutral upper segment should be used in these circumstances. Where correction for both near and distant vision is required, bifocal lenses are essential and pilots should discuss with their medical examiner the shape and size most suitable for each segment. Where triple correction is necessary for reading, the instrument panel range and distant vision, then specialist advice is required.  6.1.17 Humidity  (A) The relative humidity of cabin air is much lower in flight than what crew members are normally accustomed to. (B) Coffee and especially black coffee, being a diuretic (kidney stimulant) can exacerbate the effects of reduced humidity symptoms resulting from low humidity, like dryness of nose, mouth and throat and general fatigue. 6.1.18 Diurnal Rhythm  (A) It is a well-established fact that our bodies have a diurnal cycle or rhythm. This means that our chemical, psychological and physiological activity is low during our normal sleeping. They reach the lowest point at about 4 a.m. When we fly across time zones, either east- west or west- east, we may interrupt our diurnal cycle. However, there is no proof that this is harmful to our health. (B) To minimize the tiring effects of interruption to the diurnal rhythm, the crew members should: 1. adhere as much as possible to home time for sleeping, eating and bowel function, 2. take adequate rest before flight, and 3. eat light snacks in three or four hourly intervals to increase alertness.  6.1.19 Fatigue  (A) Flight crew duty limitations are explained in detail in   Chapter 7. (B) Any crew member shall not commence a flight duty or continue a flight duty after an intermediate landing if he is aware that he is too fatigued or will be too fatigued before next landing. (C) Cumulative fatigue, fatigue accumulated over a period of time, is also to be taken into account, when a crew member is considering his fitness for duty. (D) The basic responsibility in fatigue management rests with the individual crew member who should report for duty in a reasonably rested and fit state to perform his expected duty. This includes attention to such factors as sleep, personal fitness and health, life style and activities prior to flight. (E) If a flight crew member is not able to perform his flight duty and has a health report due to fatigue and/or exhaustion, he should fill out a Fatigue (FGR) Report on the AQD System.  6.1.20 Cosmic Radiation  (A) There are two categories of radiation, both have biological effects when they pass through body tissues: 1. non-ionizing radiation - including ultra violet light, radio waves and microwaves; and 2. ionizing radiation - including cosmic rays, x-rays and radiation from radioactive materials. (B) Cosmic radiation originates from two sources. The largest component is radiation from outer space although there is also a smaller component from the sun. The component from outer space consists of mainly high energy protons which reach the earth at a fairly constant rate. There are also lower energy protons originating from the sun although these are much less significant except when given off in bursts during solar particle events. (C) The intensity of cosmic radiation at commercial aircraft altitudes is approximately 20% higher during the solar minimum than during the solar maximum. The intensity of cosmic radiation in the earth’s atmosphere is not constant. Because the earth’s magnetic field has a higher intensity above the Equator than above the Poles, charged galactic cosmic radiation penetrates through the atmosphere more easily above the Poles than above the Equator. The intensity of cosmic radiation is therefore higher in the Polar Regions than around the Equator. The effect on the body therefore depends on the latitude and altitude at which the aircraft is flying and also the length of time of the exposure. (D) The effects of ionizing radiation depend not only on the dose absorbed, but also on the type and energy of the radiation and the tissues involved. When ionizing radiation passes through the body and energy is transmitted to the tissues, it may affect the atoms within individual cells and result in a variety of health effects including: 1. development of fatal cancer; 2. genetic risk; and 3. risk to the health of the fetus. (E) These factors are taken into account in deriving the Dose Equivalent, which is measured in Sieverts (Sv). However, doses of cosmic radiation are so low that figures are usually quoted in milliSieverts (mSv) that is thousandths of a Sievert, or microSieverts (μSv), that is millionths of a Sievert. (F) Occupational exposure for flight and cabin crew will depend on the route, altitude, and aircraft type. On average, dose rates will be in the order of: E K . 1 0 . 7 3 . 0 0 1 | R e v i s i o n 0 6 O p e r a t i o n s M a n u a l P a r t - A QMS Document Template Number: FR.18.0001 | Revision 12 Document Template Reference Document Number: TL.18.006 Page: 127 | Total Page: 466 Copy of this document has been generated on 9.01.2026 21:53. Although cosmic radiation is a form of ionizing radiation, it is impractical to consider reducing exposure by provision of shielding as one might with x-rays. Indeed, shielding may actually increase the number of secondary reaction products and thereby increase the levels of ionizing radiation. 2. Nevertheless, as will be clear from the preceding sections, it may, in principle, be possible to try to reduce exposure by changing key variables. For instance, lowering the altitude will reduce the exposure to cosmic radiation but will lengthen the flight and therefore increase the time during which the crewmember is exposed. In addition, the aircraft will also be subject to increased fuel consumption, which has other negative environmental effects. (B) Crew members should not undertake flying duties whilst under the influence of alcohol, narcotics, drugs or any medicine that was not approved by the medical department for use for crew members like sleeping tablets. (C) Any Turkish Airlines employee performing safety-sensitive functions may be subject to random drug and alcohol testing. Once notified to go for a random test, an employee is not allowed to undertake any duties without taking the drug and alcohol test. If the sickness has occurred during a domestic layover, the Station Manager completes the procedures for the crew member that needs medical attention with the Commander’s knowledge and directive, including his transfer to a State or SGK approved hospital, fills out visit and referral forms. (B) If the sickness has occurred during an international layover, the Station Manager or Local Consulate completes the procedures for the crew member that needs medical attention with the Commander’s knowledge and directive, including his transfer to a suitable hospital and fills out visit and sending forms. (C) At the end of the visit, Station Manager sends the appropriate documents to Turkish Airlines Medical Department, by the means of Flight Operations Directorate. (D) The Station Manager is responsible for making the proper arrangements to replace the sick crew member, if required.  6.2.5 Quarantine Regulations  (A) When a passenger onboard shows symptoms, which might indicate the presence of a major or suspected communicable disease, the Commander of an arriving flight must ensure that the airport medical or health authorities have been informed. Also, this information shall be notified promptly to the ATS unit during en-route by the information listed below: a) aircraft identification; b) departure aerodrome; c) destination aerodrome; d) estimated time of arrival; e) number of persons onboard f) number of suspected case(s) on board; and g) nature of the public health risk, if known. It is the responsibility of the airport medical or health authority to decide whether isolation of the aircraft, crew and passengers is necessary. FLIGHT TIME LIMITATIONS  7.1 Flight and Duty Time Limitations and Rest Requirements 7.1.1 General  All information about flight and duty time limitations and rest requirements as well as the rules about exceedances of flight duty time limitations and/or reductions of rest periods are established for all flight and cabin crew members of Turkish Airlines in compliance with national   provisions   of   Türkiye   including   Turkish   DGCA SHT-FTL Instruction   on   Flight   and   Duty   Time   Limitations   and   Resting Requirements for contributing flight safety. Relevant responsible administrative personnel and crew members that do not comply with the provisions of DK.22.059 SHT-FTL Regulation, will be penalized with administrative fines by Turkish DGCA based on Article 143 of DK.21.015 Turkish Civil Aviation Law Numbered 2920 and/or Regulation for Administrative Fines to be Issued by Turkish DGCA in   DK.22.011 SHY-İPC | Regulations On  Administrative Fines By General Directorate Of Civil Aviation. Taken into consideration the degree of defect, in case of continuation or repetition of contradictions to DK.22.059 SHT-FTL Regulation; a) Relevant administrative personnel’s authorization or certificate of approval can be suspended. b) Relevant crew members’ license or certificate can be suspended for a maximum of 6 months or completely revoked. Minimum requirements to become the Senior Vice President, Crew Planning of Turkish Airlines are: 1. Having 5 years planning or 10 years flight experience, 2. Having completed at least a 2 year university program, 3. Having completed a Fatigue Risk Management (FRM) Training Program provided by Turkish Airlines, 4. Having completed a Crew Resource Management (CRM) Training Program provided by Turkish Airlines, 5. Having completed the Flight Time Limitations (FTL) Training Program provided by Turkish DGCA, 6. Having completed the Crew Planning Training Program used by Turkish Airlines, 7. Having no definite conviction for the offenses established by Article 18 of DK.21.015 Turkish Civil Aviation Law Numbered 2920. All flights are planned as to be completed within the allowable flight duty period, taking into account the time necessary for all pre-flight duties and all subsequent flights. Within the scope of Article 7 of DK.22.059 SHT-FTL Regulation, "(1) Exceptions to the time limitation rules indicated in the DK.22.059 SHT-FTL Regulation may be permitted if operators apply to the General Directorate with detailed rationale. (2) Exceptions regarding state duties, search and rescue activities, natural disasters such as flood, fire, earthquake, etc. may be made within the scope of the permission and / or knowledge of the General Directorate.” Crew Planning Directorate shall carry out and direct all granted exceptions as well as inform other directorates accordingly. Both the individual crew members and Turkish Airlines are responsible for strict observance of these regulations. No crew member begins a flight duty period if it is foreseeable that duty time limitations as stated within this   EK.10.73.001 Operations Manual Part-A   Chapter 7 will be violated. Apart from flying for Turkish Airlines, no crew member is allowed to fly privately for financial gain, or commercially for a third party without the approval of Turkish Airlines. When undertaking duties for more than one operator by the permission of the Turkish Airlines refer to   Subchapter 7.1.5 section for details.  7.1.2 Scope  This chapter establishes the requirements to be met by Turkish Airlines and its crew members with regard to flight and duty time limitations and rest requirements for active (with a valid licence and/or certificate) flight and cabin crew members. 7.1.3 Definitions  Acclimatised : A state in which a crew member’s circadian biological clock is synchronised to the time zone where the crew member is in accordance with the values in the Table-1. A crew member is considered to be acclimatised to a 2-hour wide time zone surrounding the local time at the point of departure. When the local time at the place where a duty commences differs by more than 2 hours from the local time at the place where the next duty starts, the crew member, for the calculation of the maximum daily flight duty period, is considered to be acclimatised in accordance with the values in the Table-1: Table-1: Acclimatisation Table  Time   difference   (h) between   reference   time and local time where the crew   member   starts   the next duty Time elapsed since reporting at reference time  < 48   48 - 71:59   72 – 95:59   96 – 119:59   ≥ 120 2 < … < 4   B   D   D   D   D 4 ≤ … ≤ 6   B   X   D   D   D 6 < … ≤ 9   B   X   X   D   D 9 < … ≤ 12   B   X   X   X   D ‘B’   means acclimatised to the local time of the departure time zone, ‘D’   means acclimatised to the local time where the crew member starts his next duty, and ‘X’   means that a crew member is in an unknown state of acclimatisation. A crew member remains acclimatised to the local time of his reference time during 47 hours 59 minutes after reporting no matter how many time zones he has crossed. The maximum daily FDP for acclimatised crew members is determined by using Table-1 with the reference time of the point of departure. As soon as 48 hours have elapsed, the state of acclimatisation is derived from the time elapsed since reporting at reference time and the number of time zones crossed. A crew member is considered to be in an unknown state of acclimatisation after the first 48 hours of the rotation have elapsed unless he remains in the first arrival destination time zone (either for rest or any duties) in accordance with the Table-1. Should a crew member’s rotation include additional duties that end in a different time zone than his first arrival destination’s time zone while he is considered to be in an unknown state of acclimatisation, then the crew member remains in an unknown state of acclimatisation until he: 1. has taken the rest period required by   Subchapter 7.1.15.5 at home base; 2. has taken the rest period required by   Subchapter 7.1.15.5 at the new location; or 3. has been undertaking duties starting at and returning to the time zone of the new location until he becomes acclimatised in accordance with the values in the Table-1. To determine the state of acclimatisation, the two following criteria should be applied: E K . 1 0 . 7 3 . 0 0 1 | R e v i s i o n 0 6 O p e r a t i o n s M a n u a l P a r t - A QMS Document Template Number: FR.18.0001 | Revision 12 Document Template Reference Document Number: TL.18.006 Page: 133 | Total Page: 466 Copy of this document has been generated on 9.01.2026 21:53. The point of departure refers to the reporting point for a flight duty period or positioning duty after a rest period. The time elapsed since reporting at reference time for operations applying   Subchapter 7.1.15.5 3) (ii) at home base refers to the time elapsed since reporting for the first time at home base for a rotation.  Accommodation : For the purpose of standby and split duty, a quiet and comfortable place not open to the public with the ability to control light and temperature, equipped with adequate furniture that provides a crew member with the possibility to sleep, with enough capacity to accommodate all crew members present at the same time and with access to food and drink. Adequate furniture for crew member accommodation should include a seat that reclines at least 45° back angle to the vertical, has a seat width of at least 20 inches (50cm) and provides leg and foot support.  Airport Standby : A standby performed at the airport.  Augmented Flight Crew:   A flight crew which comprises more than the minimum number required to operate the aircraft, allowing each flight crew member to leave the assigned post, for the purpose of in-flight rest, and to be replaced by another appropriately qualified flight crew member.  Boeing Alertness Model (BAM) : Part of the Fatigue Risk Management System (FRMS) which enables Turkish Airlines to predict and control crew fatigue from a scientific point of view.  Break : A period of time within a flight duty period, shorter than a rest period, counting as duty and during which a crew member is free of all tasks.  Cabin crew member : An appropriately qualified crew member, other than a flight crew or technical crew member, who is assigned by an operator to perform duties related to the safety of passengers and flight during operations.  Call for Roster (CFR) : Local day in the roster which a duty may be assigned to a crew member via notification of IVR system or mobile platforms between 17:00 – 23:00 LT on the previous day.  Delayed Reporting : The postponement of a scheduled FDP by the operator before a crew member has left the place of rest.  Disruptive Schedule : A crew member’s roster which disrupts the sleep opportunity during the optimal sleep time window by comprising an FDP or a combination of FDPs for ‘early start’ a duty period starting in the period between 05:00 and 06:59 or for ‘late finish’ a duty period finishing in the period between 00:00 and 01:59 in the time zone to which a crew member is acclimatised.  Duty : Any task that a crew member performs for the operator, including flight duty, administrative work, giving or receiving training and checking, positioning, and some elements of standby;  Duty Period : A period which starts when a crew member is required by an operator to report for or to commence a duty and ends when that person is free of all duties, including post-flight duty.  Eastward-Westward and Westward-Eastward transition : The transition at home base between a rotation crossing 6 or more time zones in one direction and a rotation crossing 4 or more time zones in the opposite direction.  Fatigue : A physiological state of reduced mental or physical performance capability resulting from sleep loss or extended wakefulness, circadian phase, or workload (mental and/or physical activity) that can impair a crewmember’s alertness and ability to safely operate an aircraft or perform safety-related duties.  Flight crew member : A pilot licensed crew member charged with duties essential to the operation of an aircraft during a flight duty period.  Flight Duty Period (FDP) : A period that commences when a crew member is required to report for duty, which includes a sector or a series of sectors, and finishes when the aircraft finally comes to rest and the engines are shut down, at the end of the last sector on which the crew member acts as an operating crew member.  Flight (Block) Time : For aeroplanes and touring motor gliders, the time between an aircraft first moving from its parking place for the purpose of taking off until it comes to rest on the designated parking position and all engines or propellers are shut down.  FTL : Flight Time Limitations  FTSS : Flight and duty time limitations and rest requirements procedures. Home Base : The location, assigned by the operator to the crew member, from where the crew member normally starts and ends a duty period or a series of duty periods and where, under normal circumstances, the operator is not responsible for the accommodation of the crew member concerned.  IVR (Interactive Voice Response) : The electronic system that automatically notifies reserved duties of flight and cabin crew and their duty changes.  Local Day : A 24-hour period commencing at 00:00 local time.  Local Night : A period of 8 hours falling between 22:00 and 08:00 local time.  Night Duty : A duty period encroaching any portion of the period between 02:00 and 04:59 in the time zone to which the crew is acclimatised.  Operating Crew Member : A crew member carrying out duties in an aircraft during a sector. A person on board an aircraft is either a crew member or a passenger. If a crew member is not a passenger on board an aircraft he should be considered as ‘carrying out duties’. The crew member remains an operating crew member during in-flight rest. In-flight rest counts in full as FDP.  Other Standby : A standby either at home or in a suitable accommodation.  Positioning : The transferring of a non-operating crew member from one place to another, at the behest of Turkish Airlines, excluding: The time of travel from a private place of rest to the designated reporting place at home base and vice versa, and The time for local transfer from a place of rest to the commencement of duty and vice versa.  Reference Time : The local time at the reporting point situated in a 2-hour wide time zone band around the local time where a crew member is acclimatised.  Reserve : A period of time during which a crew member is required by Turkish Airlines to be available to receive an assignment for an FDP, positioning or other duty notified at least 10 hours in advance.  Rest Facility : A bunk or seat suitable for crew members’ sleeping on board an aircraft.  Rest Period : A continuous, uninterrupted and defined period of time, following duty or prior to duty, during which a crew member is free of all duties, standby and reserve.  Rotation : A duty or a series of duties, including at least one flight duty, and rest periods out of home base, starting at home base and ending when returning to home base for a rest period where Turkish Airlines is no longer responsible for the accommodation of the crew member.  Sector : The segment of an FDP between an aircraft first moving for the purpose of taking off until it comes to rest after landing on the designated parking position.  Single Day Free of Duty : A time free of all duties and standby consisting of one day and two local nights, which is notified in advance. A rest period may be included as part of the single day free of duty.  Standby : A pre-notified and defined period of time during which a crew member is required by Turkish Airlines to be available to receive an assignment for a flight, positioning or other duty without an intervening rest period;  Suitable Accommodation : For the purpose of standby, split duty, and rest, a separate room for each crew member located in a quiet environment and equipped with a bed, which is sufficiently ventilated, has a device for regulating temperature and light intensity, and access to food and drink.  Temporary Accommodation : For the purpose of rest, refers to a room having all the necessary facilities for physiological needs, such as adequate equipment for ventilation, adjustment of temperature and light intensity, and access to food and beverages, with a quiet atmosphere and at least two separate beds where up to two crew members can be accommodated.  Temporary Base : Refers to a location, apart from the main base, determined by an operator, at home or abroad, to ensure continuity of flight operations, where crew members are to be hosted for a temporary period of time, from the start date to the end date of the crew members’ flight duty period, during which the operator is obliged to provide the crew members with suitable accommodation or temporary accommodation and means of subsistence, and where an aircraft from the Turkish Airlines’ fleet that meets the minimum requirements is to be deployed.  Window of Circadian Low (WOCL) : The period between 02:00 and 05:59 hours in the time zone to which a crew member is acclimatised. 7.1.4 Turkish Airlines’ Responsibilities 7.1.4.1 General  Turkish Airlines: 1. publishes duty rosters 14 days in advance or minimum 7 days in advance covering the period of minimum 28 days in advance sufficiently to provide the opportunity for crew members to plan adequate rest; 2. ensures that flight duty periods are planned in a way that enables crew members to remain sufficiently free from fatigue so that they can operate to a satisfactory level of safety under all circumstances; 3. specifies reporting times that allow sufficient time for ground duties; 4. takes into account the relationship between the frequency and pattern of flight duty periods and rest periods and give consideration to the cumulative effects of undertaking long duty hours combined with minimum rest periods; 5. allocates duty patterns which avoid practices that cause a serious disruption of an established sleep/work pattern, such as alternating day/night duties; 6. complies with the provisions concerning disruptive schedules according to late type; 7. provides rest periods of sufficient time to enable crew members to overcome the effects of the previous duties and to be rested by the start of the following flight duty period; 8. schedules recurrent extended recovery rest periods and notify crew members sufficiently in advance; 9. schedules flight duties in order to be completed within the allowable flight duty period taking into account the time necessary for pre- flight duties, the sector and turnaround times as specified in   Subchapter 7.1.4.3; 10. changes a schedule and/or crew arrangement if the actual operation exceeds the maximum flight duty period on more than 33% of the flight duties in that schedule during a scheduled seasonal period. 11. determines, at the end of each month, the duties that exceeds the maximum FDP on more than 25% of the flight duties. Turkish Airlines categorizes such flight duties that exceeds maximum FDP by 25% in 3 consecutive months as priority flights. Turkish Airlines will alter the series of flights which include such priority flights and/or arrangements regarding flight time will be implemented in case there is no improvement on these rates at the end of 4 consecutive months at the latest. 12. sends copy of the non-conformity report to the Turkish DGCA not later than 7 business days after the event in accordance with  DK.22.121 UOD-2014/11 Reports For Submission To Flight Operations Directorate on Reports to be Sent to the Turkish DGCA Flight Operations Management. 13. does not count the medical examination days which are included in rosters of crew members as duty and/or rest period. However, Turkish Airlines plans the minimum rest time after the medical examination days in roster. 14. counts vaccination and e-learning activities which are included in rosters of crew members as a duty period.  7.1.4.2 Scheduling  Flight duties and/or other duties are scheduled by Turkish Airlines’ Crew Planning Directorate. The final responsibility rests with the Nominated Person for Crew Planning and Accountable Manager. 1. Scheduling has an important impact on a crew member’s ability to sleep and to maintain a proper level of alertness. When developing a workable roster, Turkish Airlines strikes a fair balance between the commercial needs and the capacity of individual crew members to work effectively. Rosters are developed in such a way that they distribute the amount of work evenly among those that are involved. 2. Schedules allow for flights to be completed within the maximum permitted flight duty period and flight rosters take into account the time needed for pre-flight duties, taxiing, the flight- and turnaround times. Other factors to be considered when planning duty periods include: the allocation of work patterns which avoid undesirable practices such as alternating day/night duties, alternating eastward- westward or westward-eastward time zone transitions, positioning of crew members so that a serious disruption of established sleep/work patterns occurs; Scheduling sufficient rest periods especially after long flights crossing many time zones; and E K . 1 0 . 7 3 . 0 0 1 | R e v i s i o n 0 6 O p e r a t i o n s M a n u a l P a r t - A QMS Document Template Number: FR.18.0001 | Revision 12 Document Template Reference Document Number: TL.18.006 Page: 136 | Total Page: 466 Copy of this document has been generated on 9.01.2026 21:53. Preparation of duty rosters sufficiently in advance with planning of recurrent extended recovery rest periods and notification of the crew members well in advance to plan adequate pre-duty rest.  7.1.4.3 Operational Robustness  Turkish Airlines establishes and monitors performance indicators for operational robustness of rosters. Performance indicators for operational robustness of rosters support Turkish Airlines in the assessment of the stability of its rostering system. Performance indicators for operational robustness of rosters at least measure how often a rostered crew pairing for a duty period is achieved within the planned duration of that duty period. Crew pairing means rostered positioning and flights for crew members in one duty period. The planning of crew schedules is done according to the limitation defined in this section. The performance indicator for Turkish Airlines is the FDP limits and they are monitored before and through the crew operation and necessary actions are taken in reasonable time frame if possible. Turkish Airlines can only take the responsibility of the controllable factors which are: Scheduled block times Scheduled turnaround times Known airport and en-route traffic conditions On the other hand, the following factors but not limited to be out of control of Turkish Airlines: Adverse weather conditions Industrial Action Political Unrest / Civil Unrest / Terrorist Activity Force Majeure Service / Infrastructure failure of external / Independent agencies e.g. ATC/SITA, etc. Reactionary delay / Diversion e.g. medical / Unruly passenger etc.  7.1.5 Crew Member Responsibilities  Crew members shall: 1. comply with: comply with all flight and duty time limitations (FTL) and rest requirements applicable to their activities. when undertaking duties for more than one operator by the permission of the Turkish Airlines: maintain his individual records regarding flight and duty times and rest periods as referred to in applicable FTL requirements; and provide each operator with the date needed to schedule activities in accordance with the applicable FTL requirements. The crew member shall not perform duties on an aircraft: if he knows or suspects that he is suffering from fatigue or feels otherwise unfit, to the extent that the flight may be endangered. 2. Make optimum use of the opportunities and facilities for rest provided and plan and use their rest periods properly.  7.1.6 Fatigue Risk Management (FRM)  See   EK.10.21.001 Safety Management Manual Chapter 5.
