9.2.1 General  For transportation of weapons of war and munitions of war permission must be granted by the States concerned, including those being over-flown.  9.2.1.1 Weapons of War or Munitions of War  Must be stowed in the aeroplane in a place which is inaccessible to passengers during flight, firearms must not be loaded. Exceptions may be granted by all States concerned before the commencement of the flight that such weapons of war or munitions of war may be carried in circumstances that differ in part or in total from the procedures mentioned in this paragraph above.  9.2.1.2 Sporting Weapons  (A) There is no internationally agreed definition of sporting weapons. In general, they may be any weapons, which is not a weapon of war or munitions of war. Specifically, a firearm, which is not a weapon of war or munitions of war, should be treated as a sporting weapon for the purpose of its carriage on an aeroplane. (B) Sporting weapons include hunting knives, bows and other similar articles. (C) Turkish Airlines shall take all reasonable measures to ensure that he will be informed about any intended transportation of any sporting weapons or ammunition by one of his aeroplanes. (D) A firearm is any gun, rifle or pistol which fires a projectile and the following firearms are generally regarded as being sporting weapons: 1. Those designated for shooting game, birds and other animals 2. Those used for target shooting, clay-pigeon shooting and competition shooting 3. Air guns, dart guns, starting pistols, etc. (E) Sporting rifles, shotguns and pistols belonging to accompanying passengers for their own use, and any other kind of small arms may not be carried aboard the aeroplane except as checked baggage stowed in one of the belly compartments, not loaded and suitably packed.  9.2.1.3 Accepting the Carriage of Sporting Weapons and Ammunition  When accepting the carriage of sporting weapons, Turkish Airlines shall ensure that they are: 1. stowed in the aeroplane in a place which is inaccessible to passengers during flight unless the Turkish DGCA has determined that compliance is impracticable and has accepted that other procedures might apply; 2. unloaded, in the case of firearms or other weapons that can contain ammunition; and 3. securely packed ammunition in Division 1.4S may be carried in quantities not exceeding 5 kg gross weight per person for that own person’s use, excluding ammunition with explosive or incendiary projectiles. Allowance for more than one passenger must not be combined into one or more packages.  9.2.2 Information to Commander  Before the flight, the Commander must be notified by the ground handling staff of details of weapons or ammunition intended to be carried on board, including its location.  9.2.3 Acceptance and Transportation of Armed Individuals and Their Weapons  (A) Turkish Airlines complies with the provisions of international and local regulations regarding the carriage of armed individuals and their weapons. Turkish Airlines does not allow the carriage of weapons in the cabin. However, an exemption can be made only if additional conditions specified in   DK.22.111 National Civil Aviation Security Programme (MSHGP) and Turkish Airlines EK.10.15.001  Security Program Chapter 3.11.1. Carriage of Weapons under Authorization are met accordingly; Turkish Airlines ensures that: 1. Turkish Airlines representative processing an armed passenger reviews the armed individual's credentials. These credentials must include a full-face picture of the armed individual, the signature of the authorizing officer and the official seal of the armed individual's service. 2. The Commander is notified about the individual's name, location in the airplane, and status in the remarks section of the notification to captain form, and/or similar written form, i.e., "armed individual", "escort", "armed individual travelling with persons subject of judicial or administrative proceedings" etc. E K . 1 0 . 7 3 . 0 0 1 | R e v i s i o n 0 6 O p e r a t i o n s M a n u a l P a r t - A QMS Document Template Number: FR.18.0001 | Revision 12 Document Template Reference Document Number: TL.18.006 Page: 401 | Total Page: 466 Copy of this document has been generated on 9.01.2026 21:53. SECURITY  10.1 General Security Instructions  (A) This chapter complies with National and International Regulations in accordance with   DK.22.111 National Civil Aviation Security  Programme (MSHGP) and Turkish Airlines   EK.10.15.001 Security Program. (B) See   EK.10.15.001 Security Program Chapter 11 for the details of the required Security Trainings of Crew Members.  10.1.1. Identification Cards  (A) Each crew member must wear the Turkish Airlines issued Identification Card (ID card) containing his photo for the duration of active duty. 1. The ID card shall be visible at all times: a. When on active duty, or b. When entering areas requiring the display of the ID card. (B) ID card must not be lent or disposed of in any manner. (C) If the ID card is lost, it must immediately be reported to the Turkish Airlines Security Directorate, Facilities Security Management and a replacement ID card shall be obtained. (D) On board the parked aircraft, during duty period, cabin crew are responsible for checking the identity of the persons on board.If cabin crew is not present, the flight crew is responsible for checking the identity of the persons on board. The identification check includes the check of the fields, numbers, or names that indicate whether the person who will enter is authorized to enter this area and the validity of this authorization, the check of the expiration date of the ID cards, and the check of whether the picture on the card matches the card holder. In case any exceptional situation stemming from the local authority in relation to ID check, the station officials should inform the flight crew and the cabin crew of the application verbally.  10.1.2 Crew Members Baggage Security  (A) Crew members must not leave their baggage unattended at any time. (B) Crew members must not accept sealed parcels for carriage from third parties. (C) Crew members shall not entrust any packages to other crew members. (D) Crew members shall only carry on board an aeroplane their own personal baggage. (E) All crew members are responsible for the handling and security of their own personal baggage. (B) The identification of all persons (non-passenger) boarding an aeroplane shall be checked: 1. Identification by Airport Entrance Card, which must be visibly worn, is regarded as sufficient. (C) Objects taken into the flight deck or cabin shall be checked by the cabin crew. (D) Passenger belongings, which have been security checked do not require a re-check. (E) Checking the integrity of the seals on catering equipment is regarded to be sufficient, but spot checks of the contents are required. (F) For transit passengers refer to   Subchapter 8.2.2.1.2 (G) Security authorities must be informed immediately when any doubt exists as to: 1. The authorization of any person to enter an aeroplane; 2. Doubt in identity; 3. Refusal of identity-check; and 4. Suspicion of any act or deed of jeopardizing the security of the aeroplane. (H) All crew members shall support security authorities, when required.  10.1.8.2 Principles for Securing of Parked Aeroplane Not Under Crew Members Supervision  (A) If Turkish Airlines contracted maintenance personnel is available, the responsibility for security of the aeroplane is automatically transferred to the respective organization. (B) If Turkish Airlines contracted ground operations personnel and ground power are available, the responsibility for security of the aeroplane is automatically transferred to the respective organization after all type related checklists to secure and power down the aeroplane are completed by the flight crew members, allowing the ground power/main bus remains available for ground services continuing on aircraft. (C) If Turkish Airlines contracted ground operations personnel is available but no ground power is connected, the responsibility for security of the aeroplane is automatically transferred to the respective organization after all type related checklists to secure and power down the aeroplane are completed by the flight crew members. The Duty Flight Operations Manager shall contact the Senior Vice President, Security and advise the Commander. Together they will assess the situation. If deemed necessary or in order to obtain additional information/ guidance, Turkish DGCA may be contacted through the Senior Vice President, Security. The Flight and Cabin Crew shall carry out a complete security search of the aircraft using the Detailed List of Areas to be Searched According to   FR.73.0001 Aircraft Security Search Checklist. 2. If all searches are completed with no irregularities, the aeroplane can be released for flight. However, the Senior Vice President, Security or the Commander can impose any additional measures deemed necessary in the given circumstances.  10.1.9 Aircraft Security in Flight  Turkish Airlines shall take all measures to ensure that no person is in any part of an aeroplane in flight which is not a part designed for the accommodation of persons unless temporary access has been granted by the Commander to any part of the aeroplane: 1. For the purpose of taking action necessary for the security of the aeroplane or of any person, animal or goods therein, or 2. In which cargo or stores are carried, being a part which is designed to enable a person to have access thereto while the aeroplane is in flight.  10.1.10. Aircraft Security Search  (A) Aircraft security search means a through inspection of the interior and exterior of the aircraft for the purpose of discovering suspicious objects, weapons, explosives or other dangerous devices, articles or substances. However, a threat evaluation must be performed within the framework of certain procedures. The Commander must be notified of the found objects. Cabin chief/crew performs an evaluation according to procedures described in EK.10.71.001 Cabin Crew Manual Chapter 10.2.11. Unclaimed and Left (Found) Property on Board/Suspicious Object with the definition given below, and notifies the Commander about the result whether the object is identified as a suspicious object or found property. (B)   Suspicious Object: On the Ground before boarding / after deboarding; On the Ground after boarding / During Flight including taxi; During TRANSIT after passenger baggage reconciliation if the item represents one or more of the following descriptions;  (a) Properties, objects, packages and/or all the electronic devices that appear to be tampered, the contents of which cannot be seen and/or identified clearly through external visual check, which emit sounds and/or odors, which vibrate and/or leak fluids, which cables, ropes/strings, etc. stick out from, (b) Toys that have mechanisms and are convenient to place item(s) inside in terms of their features and physical structures, packages, items, and objects that raise the suspicion of being left intentionally and are not regarded as Unclaimed and Left (Found) Item. Note: Note  Note 1 : Electronic devices that are shorter than 16 cm, narrower than 9 cm, thinner than 1.5 cm and have no signs of tampering are not deemed suspicious object. Unclaimed and Forgotten (Found) Properties Left Onboard/Suspicious Objects.  10.2 Determination of the Seriousness of an Act of Unlawful Interference 10.2.1 Unlawful Interference  (A) The   DK.21.301 Tokyo Convention On Offences And Certain Other Acts Committed On Board Aircraft of 1963 defines illegal interference with international civil aviation as “acts which, whether or not they are offences, may or do jeopardize the safety of the aircraft or of persons or property therein or which jeopardize good order and discipline on board". (B) However, from the crew perspective, the three major forms of unlawful interference are: 1. Unruly passenger, 2. Hijacking, and 3. Bomb threat.  10.2.2 Unruly/Disruptive Passenger  (A) Individual passengers or groups of passengers who fail to respect the rules of conduct on board an aircraft or to follow the instructions of crew members and thereby disturb the good order and discipline on board aircraft with the potential to behave in an unruly manner. (B) The success of preventive strategy relies on three conditions; 1. Raised awareness among passengers of how the Turkish Airlines will respond to disruptive acts; 2. The implementation of a zero-tolerance policy; and 3. The likelihood and type of consequence in response to their disruptive behaviors. (C) Many unruly passenger incidents, even some of those which reach to level 3 or level 4, are initiated by passengers with personality disorders. It is therefore important that the cabin crew be able to recognize these disorders and to interact effectively with these individuals. (D) In conclusion, Turkish Airlines implementation of an effective strategy on the handling of unruly passengers based on the enforcement of a zero-tolerance policy, crew training and, where warranted, on board enforcement of good order and discipline are the tools needed for the assured prevention of escalation from a non-terrorist level1 passenger disturbance to a level 3 or level 4 disturbance.  10.2.2.1 Levels of Threat  (A) Crew familiarity with basic threat levels history and potential can provide variable tools to aid them in their earliest determination of the seriousness of an incident. For successful handling of occurrences of unlawful interference, the development of a close working relationship between Turkish Airlines management, Flight Operations Directorate and individual flight and cabin crew members is established and a relationship based on realistic trust and credibility between all these parties is achieved. Threat Level 3: Life-threatening behavior. 4. Any threat to enter the flight deck is very serious and should be considered as a method of gaining control of the aircraft and use it as a mass destruction weapon. Flight crew should use an emergency or rapid descend to minimize the time of exposure to the hijack in flight. 3. A hijacker would most probably immobilize a pilot by attacking him on the head, neck and throat from the blind side. If the assailant has gained access to the flight deck, one of the flight crew should take all necessary measures to prevent the assailant from taking control or causing the flight crew to lose control of the aircraft, while the pilot flying maintains control of the aircraft. 4. Cabin crew should in such cases act early and use all resources available to prevent an assailant gaining access to the flight crew compartment. Expect   interception   by   military   aircraft   and   monitor   the frequency 121.5 Follow intercept procedures as appropriate.  10.2.2.3 Restraint Procedure  (A) Crew immunity for actions taken against a perpetrator; 1. The   DK.21.301 Tokyo Convention On Offences And Certain Other Acts Committed On Board Aircraft of 1963, which specifically addresses illegal interference with international civil aviation, provides immunity for actions taken against a perpetrator. In particular, Article 10 states that “For actions taken in accordance with this Convention, neither the aircraft Commander, any other member of the crew, any passenger, the owner or operator of the aircraft, nor the person on whose behalf the flight was performed shall be held responsible in any proceeding on account of the treatment undergone by the person against whom the actions were taken” 2. In any developing incident in the cabin, the flight crew should be notified of the type and level of the threat, the number of perpetrators, any weapons, assigned seat numbers, and physical description(s) of the perpetrator(s). 3. At the first indication that an incident may start to erupt, immediate lockdown of the flight crew compartment should occur. Should the incident appear to advance to a Level 3 or Level 4 incident, passengers should be in their seats, a galley cart placed in front of the flight crew compartment door and ABPs should be requested to block the flight crew compartment door area. It is far better to be overly cautious than to wait and see what develops. (B) Restraining: 1. Cabin crew should be well trained in the application of restraint devices, such as plastic "flex cuffs" so as to have the capability to maintain control over an aggressive perpetrator. To ensure successful application of such control devices, ideally four cabin crew member and/or able-bodied passengers (ABPs) should be involved. One person for each foot, one for each hand, and one to apply the device. Care must be exercised to ensure that the cuffs are applied correctly. Too loose, and they can be ineffective; too tight, and they can injuriously limit circulation. These devices, belts, or other restraints should be applied with the perpetrator's hands secured behind the individual's body. The more detailed information can be found in EK.10.71.001 Cabin Crew Manual Chapter 10.6. Physical Restraint. 2. The use of handcuffs may only be authorized by the Commander except in only some extreme situations the cabin chief may decide to handcuff a passenger, should there be no time to advise the Commander and if security is threatened. The cabin chief will be held responsible when restraining a passenger without prior approval from the Commander. 3. Handcuffing of a person will most probably require the support of several assistants as resistance is to be expected. 4. The cabin chief has to coordinate the necessary actions by giving precise instructions to the crew and asking passengers for assistance. 5. The following rules must be considered when applying handcuffs a. Do not lay the person on the floor, in order to avoid "suffocation". b. Do not use an additional gag to silence the person. c. Call for a doctor if deemed necessary. Commander shall decide whether or not an unruly passenger FR.73.0031  On-Board Unruly Passenger Report (On the Ground / In – Flight) form shall be filled out and signed by the cabin chief. Forms shall be distributed to the relevant units mentioned on the bottom of the form, after Commander approval (signature). FR.73.0066 On Ground/In-Flight Incident Report can also be filled in Turkish language for inbound flights to Türkiye. (B) After the person has been handed over to the proper authorities, the Commander shall not be related in any way to the procedures/trial to follow in any country including the Republic of Türkiye. Turkish Airlines Legal & Compliance Directorate shall handle this procedure so that the plaintiff is Turkish Airlines and not the applicable Commander. (C) In case of urgency, IOCC shall be notified via telephone. For reporting situations, refer to   Chapter 11. (D) These forms should also be located within the cabin to prevent opening of the cockpit door.  10.2.3 Hijacking  (A) Differentiation between “an ongoing attempted hijacking” and a “hijacking” is a most important distinction as regards aircraft external response. An “ongoing attempted hijacking” is just that; the flight crew is still in control of the aircraft. A “hijacking” means that; the hijackers is in control of the aircraft, it is absolutely essential that the flight crew clarify this distinction with Air Traffic Control (ATC), due to the potential difference in response and resultant risk variables to all on board the aircraft. (B) A critical distinction to be made is “attempted hijack” versus “suspected hijack” versus “hijack”. While each may have quite different meaning to the on-board crew, an aircraft that has clearly diverted from its planned route of flight, is proceeding toward a major population center and is not in communication with ground entities may well be treated as a hijacking with intended use as a weapon of mass destruction. The potential cost of allowing the flight crew compartment door to be breached by a suicidal terrorist team must be very clearly communicated in flight to both the cabin crew and the Flight Crew.  10.2.3.1 Stages of Hijack  (A) As long as the aeroplane being hijacked is still on the ground, the Flight Crew shall not take-off. (B) In case of a hijacking when airborne: 1. Everything will be done to hinder the hijacker in getting access to the flight deck. 2. The Flight Crew must maintain control of the flight deck under all circumstances. 3. Should any person be held hostage in the cabin in an attempt to gain access to the flight deck, the flight deck door shall be kept closed and locked. 4. The Flight Crew will land the aeroplane as soon as possible at a suitable airport. (C) After landing the aeroplane will be parked so that a succeeding take-off is prevented. (D) The aeroplane should be configured such as that another flight is made impossible (e.g., blowing the engine fire extinguishers, but not the APU so that people can have air condition and electricity/Excerpt from ICAO Manual on the implementation of the security provisions of   DK.31.023 ICAO Annex 6 | Operation Of Aircraft - Aeroplanes (Part I/Part II).) (E) Any employee receiving information about the hijacking of an aeroplane operated by Turkish Airlines should immediately inform IOCC, who will then initiate the Turkish Airlines emergency procedure. IOCC will then try to contact the crew via any means possible direct or via stations en-route. (F) The cabin crew will inform the Flight Crew as soon as possible via interphone about an aggressor in the cabin. This should make the Flight Crew aware of the situation, the flight deck door will be kept closed and locked and a landing at the nearest suitable airport will be initiated. (G) The cabin crew should be aware of the fact that additional hijackers may be hidden among the passengers. Cabin crew must try to keep calm, try to de-escalate and they must make clear to the hijacker that access to the flight deck will not be possible. (H) During an extended hijacking, members of the crew should rest in shifts to be alert when on duty and possibly attempt to wear the hijacker out. One member of the cabin crew should always be with the hijacker, in order to obtain information upon which the Commander can base further decisions. (I) In order to prevent hijacking and sabotage, a set of precautionary measures has been established, which can be varied according to the actual threat situation by decision of the Company, in cooperation with the local police authority. The flight crew is to remain on the flight deck at all times. If, in spite of adherence to all security procedures, a hijacker should succeed in entering the flight deck, try to prevent the seat of an active crew member being occupied by the hijacker. Use careful but firm behavior. Such a capture is very risky, especially when an intentional intervention with the operation of the aeroplane is involved. An attempt to disarm or to disable the hijacker shall only be made if this action is deemed to be the adequate measure to avoid a disaster. Commanders are discouraged from special aeroplane maneuvers in order to overcome hijackers. This restriction, however, does not exclude emergency descent procedures, which might be necessary in order to evade the risk involved in a possible explosion. (B) Should the hijacker give instructions to divert to another destination, calculate a fuel flight plan to the hijack destination. Arguing with armed hijackers should only be attempted if the demanded “diversion” involves substantial risks due to fuel reserves, airfield conditions, etc. (C) If possible establish discreet Air Ground Communication. If plain language is permitted the flight crew will give the status of flight to ATC and as much information as deemed helpful. It should be stated whether violence has taken place on board. (D) Switch transponder to code 7500 – international code to signal a hijack. If not under radar control, transmit in an air/ground message the call sign followed by “Transponder code seven five zero zero”. Controllers will acknowledge receipt of code 7500 by asking if this is intentional. The Commander need only to reply "affirm" and proper authorities will be notified. Switch transponder code from 7500 to 7700 to signal “situation appears desperate, need all possible assistance”. This will alert all concerned that intervention may be required upon landing. If not under radar control, verbally transmit call sign followed “transponder seven-seven-zero-zero”. When changing from 7500 to 7700 wait until code 7500 is acknowledged by the controller. Controller will also acknowledge receipt of code 7700.  10.2.3.3 Phases  (A) Intimidation Phase; 1. Hijacker Characteristics; a. Instill Fear b. Violent, aggressive, emotional, nervous 2. Aims to: a. Establish control b. Prevent Counteraction c. Be respected 3. Passenger & Crew Characteristics; a. Fear, panic, disbelief, anger 4. Aims to: a. 'Be a good Hostage' b. 'Be Grey' (to be Inconspicuous) c. Move to 'Custodial Phase', as quickly as possible! The definition and appropriate Turkish Airlines response are detailed below:  Inappropriate remark : This is defined as any remark made to, or overheard by any Turkish Airlines Employee which indicates a person may be carrying a bomb (or other such explosive device), a firearm or weapon regardless of that person’s intent or reason for making the comment or statement. The response to this situation will depend upon where in the process of travel the passenger is. Anywhere of the aircraft will be dealt with by Commercial Services. Embarkation or Disembarkation: If a crewmember is alerted by an “inappropriate remark” from a passenger, the cabin chief and Commander will be informed immediately. The passenger and baggage will be removed from the aircraft and the Commander will inform the Airport Duty Manager or the local handling agent who will escort the passenger away from the aircraft. Where possible the Operations Duty Manager should be informed of the situation. The passenger will be denied boarding or return travel. In Flight: The cabin chief and Commander will be informed. The Commander has the authority to initiate an immediate diversion, or continue to destination depending on the nature of the remark, and the subsequent actions of the passenger concerned. In either case every effort should be made to alert the Operations Duty Manager or a local handling agent of the situation, and the need to have the passenger escorted from the aircraft. (B) Over 99% of bomb threat calls against civil aviation targets are hoaxes, perpetrated by people who wish to cause a nuisance and/or disruption to normal activity at airports or air carrier operations. The level of disruption caused will vary according to the severity of the threat and the scale of reaction to it. Disruption may cause significant delay to services and inconvenience and probably discomfort and unease to airport, air carrier and customers. The costs of such disruption can be significant. Bomb warnings are normally anonymous telephone calls which may provide information indicating the intention to commit an act of terrorism or sabotage against an air carrier, aircraft or airport installation. Written warnings are rare but should be assessed using the same techniques as applied to a telephoned warning. Telephoned bomb warnings may be received by airports or air carriers either directly from the people using the warnings or from intermediaries, for example, press agencies or the media. Because it is practically impossible to determine if a really dangerous situation exists or if it is only an empty threat, every bomb threat must be taken seriously. (C) In the Republic of Türkiye, it is the responsibility of the airport and security authorities to carry out the correct measures and the examination of the aeroplane and the facilities for protection against sabotage. Turkish Airlines must ask and allow examination and assist with its own staff. A requested assistance is to be performed by the station engineer/aircraft technician. Outside Türkiye the respective local rules apply. If an examination of technical areas of the aeroplane is required, a station engineer shall be called in. If in a station not having technical personnel then Pilot in Command will advise the security officials for the examination of the aircraft. When outside Türkiye, also consider informing or having the Turkish Diplomatic Mission informed. In exceptional cases, for example, when in an isolated airfield, the Commander decides further actions. (D) When information about a bomb threat is received, IOCC must be notified immediately. IOCC, then, will proceed accordingly. Turkish Airlines Senior Vice President Security, Senior Vice President Flight Operations, Senior Vice President Ground Operations, Senior Vice President Corporate Safety should then be informed, as per   PR.15.028 Aviation Security Threat Assessment Procedure Section 6.1 Bomb Threat Notices.  10.2.4.2 Classification of Threats  (A) Threats are classified as   RED, AMBER or GREEN . The action to be taken depends upon the class into which the threat falls and the experience of the person responsible for making the evaluation. (B) For a threat to be classified as   “RED”   the information received must be sufficient to identify a particular flight or installation and to indicate that a bomb or device is on board or has been planted. (C) For a threat to be classified as   “AMBER”   the threat should be non-specific and could relate to any number of targets, but where, despite their general nature, it is considered prudent to take extra precautions on departing flights. These precautions could include the pre-departure screening of all baggage and cargo for example. (D) For a threat to be classified as   “GREEN”   the information received must be of a general nature such that it is not possible, even by inference, to identify any particular flight or installation.  10.2.4.3 “Red" Bomb Threat  (A)   When a bomb threat or warning is associated with an aeroplane on the ground:  1. Before boarding: a. Leave the aeroplane with your cabin baggage. 2. During boarding: a. Stop boarding; 1. Disembark passengers with all cabin baggage via stairs or jetties, and 2. Leave the aeroplane. 3. During taxi: a. Taxi to a designated parking position if such a position is available, or b. Taxi to a remote and isolated location which is apart from buildings and/or aeroplane movement areas. 1. Then, disembark the passengers via stairs. 2. Escape slides should only be used in extreme conditions. 3. Then, leave the aeroplane. 4. When you leave the aeroplane, make sure that the parking brake is not set. 10.2.5 Dealing with Chemical / Biological Weapon (CBW)  In this section, information will be introduced about Chemical / Biological Weapon (CBW). The situation is similar to above subject. Principally, almost same operational procedures will be applied. A critical distinction to be made is the difference between the handling of a bomb and CBW.  10.2.5.1 Aerosol CBW Activation  A primary method of distributing chemical and biologic agents inside the aircraft is aerosol dispersion. The action of leaking, exploding, or manually pouring the substance into the cabin interior will move the agent through simple airborne transmission onto the skin or into the eyes, lungs and nasal passages. It will be the goal of crew members to contain the weapon's aerosol potential before it spreads through the cabin atmosphere or, if unable, to minimize its effect on passengers and crew.  10.2.5.2 CBW Threats in Cabin - Without Activation  (A) If a CBW is reported to be on aircraft -but without apparent activation due lack of physical symptoms or exposure- it should be noted that exposure to biological agents will not likely result in an immediate presence of symptoms; nor will the dispersal of a biological or chemical agent necessarily be immediately detectable. The crew must take immediate steps to deal with the situation and attempt to minimize aerosol dispersion immediately. Flight and cabin crew have different duties that should be started simultaneously. (B) Flight crew should immediately don masks, goggles, select 100% oxygen, minimize skin coverage with shirt sleeves down or uniform jackets worn. Some CBW agents are odorless and will not be sensed until it is too late, so this step should not be delayed. Although an emergency declaration and turn towards an alternate aerodrome is appropriate, an immediate change in cabin pressure should not be initiated until the inactivated device is secured to the maximum extent possible. Immediately reducing cabin temperature to the lowest practical setting and turning off recirculation fans / cabin fans will decrease most aerosol dispersion characteristics. (C) Once the suspected Chemical/Biological container is covered and sealed from the cabin atmosphere, a gradual descent of the aircraft can be initiated using a descent that minimizes the rate of cabin change. The slower the descent and increase in cabin pressure, the lower the risk of agent dispersal during the final phase of flight. (D)   CBW in Cabin but Inactivated:  1. Don mask and goggles, 2. Inform ATC and declare emergency, squawk 7700, 3. Do not change altitude until procedure directs, 4. Turn off recirculation fans /cabin fans, decrease cabin temperature, 5. Attempt to contain/wrap device, 6. Consider turning the passenger oxygen switch on, 7. Initiate slow descent to appropriate alternate aerodrome, 8. Quarantine passengers upwind of aircraft until assistance arrives.  10.2.5.3 CBW Threats in Cabin - With Activation  (A) With the exception of slow-acting biological agents, such as anthrax, airborne exposure to toxic agents may rapidly generate sudden passenger sickness in an epidemic outbreak. Generally, many biological agents will generate symptoms less rapidly then will chemical agents, many of which cause immediate symptoms. Depending on the agent, passenger and cabin crew may exhibit choking, discoloration and fainting, blistering or convulsions that are beyond the means of crew members to effectively deal with while airborne. (B) Flight crew members must don mask and goggles before any other action. Turn on the passenger oxygen switch. Secure the cabin door and deny any entry from the cabin. Next, decrease cabin pressure -by raising the cabin altitude- as quickly as possible, to evacuate and dilute the aerosol chemical agent. Recirculation fans/cabin fans should be turned off and the coldest possible temperature should be selected to aid in minimizing agent aerosol dispersion. Cabin crew and passengers should go on oxygen. A rapid descent and an immediate landing paramount to ensure flight crew are physically able to land the aircraft and gain time-critical medical treatment for exposed individuals. (C)   CBW In Cabin but Activated:  1. Don mask and goggles, 2. 3. Inform ATC and declare emergency, squawk 7700, 4. Turn off recirculation fans/cabin fans, 5. Raise cabin elevation to 10 000 feet at fastest rate possible, 6. Decrease cabin temperature coolest possible, 7. Execute emergency descent procedure, 8. Upon landing, evacuate aircraft via upwind side of aeroplane, 9. Quarantine passengers upwind of aircraft until assistance arrives.  10.2.5.4 CBW Threat in Cargo Compartment  (A) A reported CBW threat in cargo compartment should be dealt with much as one would deal with a cargo fire: isolate the cargo bay by removing all sources of ventilation and turn off recirculation fans/cargo fans. In-flight activation of a CBW may be sensed by smoke detectors in the cargo hold. Normal firefighting techniques will provide optimal protection. During descent, a positive outflow of pressure from the air-conditioning packs will decrease the risk of chemical agents migrating from the cargo bays and into the cabin. Setting the landing elevation lower than the actual destination will keep the cabin relatively over-pressurized throughout the landing phase. Manually keeping outflow valves from fully opening upon landing could keep the cabin over-pressurized and protected from cargo area contamination until ready for emergency evacuation through upwind exits. (B) CBW in cargo Hold 1. Don mask and goggles, 2. Inform ATC and declare emergency, squawk 7700, 3. Turn off recirculation fans/cabin fans, 4. Accomplish cargo fire checklist, 5. Consider turning the passenger oxygen switch on, 6. Maintain positive cabin pressure until landing, 7. Stop aircraft with surface wind at 10/2 o'clock position, 8. Evacuate aircraft via upwind side of aeroplane, 9. Quarantine passengers upwind of aircraft until assistance arrives  10.2.5.5 Brief Information for Landing After a CBW Threat  In any CBW threat situation, do not taxi to a terminal area after landing, but instead seek a location downwind of any populated structures. The aircraft should be parked diagonally to reported surface winds and disembarkation should be undertaken only on the upwind side of the aircraft. All passengers and crew should be kept together and quarantined from non-emergency personnel.  10.3 Crew Communication, Coordination and Responses  (A) The good communication and interaction between the flight and cabin crew has a strong and positive influence not only flight safety but also on the quality of service that an operator can provide. The environment created by the closed and locked flight crew compartment door makes this concept more important than ever before and its implementation more challenging. A major concern of crew members in regard to the closed and locked flight crew compartment door, particularly during a “lockdown” situation is the loss of face-to-face interaction between all elements of the crew. There must, therefore, be effective means of interphone communication. Back up communications procedures for use in the event of inability of cabin crew to speak freely via the interphone must be established during the pre-flight briefing. (B) Briefing by the Commander during security threatening situations shall include: 1. security briefing items; 2. security information (i.e., Country specification etc.); 3. crew communication; E K . 1 0 . 7 3 . 0 0 1 | R e v i s i o n 0 6 O p e r a t i o n s M a n u a l P a r t - A QMS Document Template Number: FR.18.0001 | Revision 12 Document Template Reference Document Number: TL.18.006 Page: 431 | Total Page: 466 Copy of this document has been generated on 9.01.2026 21:53. 4. security procedure; and 5. special attention passengers.  10.3.1 Crew Response and Actions  (A) Early recognition of a threat, intervention and removal while at the gate can preclude a serious on-board incident. Similarly, observation of the passengers as they board the aircraft may provide another opportunity to solve a problem while still on the ground. Initial Flight Crew actions may include observation of the passengers as they board and then support of the cabin crew in their concerns of evident threat. (B) The crew response should be appropriate to the level of threat. All four threat levels have certain responses in common. Each escalation in threat level, however, calls for escalating responses. As the crew must operate together as a unit, suggested in-flight responses are integrated as shown in   Subchapter 10.2.2.2. These lists can be logically adapted for use at the gate, taxi and in-flight.  10.4 Post - Incident Concerns for Crew  (A) The flight crew shall cooperate with the Authorities. (B) If in a foreign country, contact the airline representative, follow Turkish Airlines procedures. (C) Do not discuss the situation with the media or other witness. (D) All crew members who have been involved or witnessed the incident involving passenger disturbance (Level 1-4) must forward a written statement to the authorities and Turkish Airlines as required. (E) Collect all necessary information from the witnesses including contact information. (F) Treat all security information confidentially and provide information only to those who operationally require it. Expect that the whole crew might have to remain at the airport until all required coordination has been completed with the authorities and the airline.  10.5 Cyber Threats, Critical Aviation Information and Communication Technology Systems  Turkish Airlines   ensures   the   necessary   measures   to   be   taken   against   cyber   threats/attacks. HANDLING, NOTIFYING AND REPORTING ACCIDENTS, INCIDENTS AND OCCURRENCES AND USING THE CVR RECORDING  11.1   Handling,   Notifying   and   Reporting   Accidents,   Incidents   and   Occurrences   and   Using   the   CVR Recording 11.1.1 Introduction  Flight Safety is the number one priority for Turkish Airlines. Reporting of accidents, incidents, occurrences and others listed in SRS (confidential, hazard and fatigue etc.) improves flight safety by correlating the data and identifying potential problem areas. As such, reporting of all incidents and accidents should be considered of utmost importance and flight crew members are encouraged to submit a written report when an occurrence that could potentially have an adverse effect on the safety of flight operations has been observed. The Safety Policy clearly represents Turkish Airlines’ perspective on Safety. The original document may be reached through DDMS PL.10.21.001 Safety Policy and Corporate Safety Directorate Web page ( safety.thy.com).  11.1.2 Definitions  Occurrence:   Means an operational interruption, defect, fault or other irregular circumstance that has or may have influenced operational safety.  Incident:   An occurrence, other than an accident, associated with the operation of an aircraft which affects or could affect the safety of operation.  Serious Incident:   An incident involving circumstances indicating that an accident nearly occurred. E K . 1 0 . 7 3 . 0 0 1 | R e v i s i o n 0 6 O p e r a t i o n s M a n u a l P a r t - A QMS Document Template Number: FR.18.0001 | Revision 12 Document Template Reference Document Number: TL.18.006 Page: 432 | Total Page: 466 Copy of this document has been generated on 9.01.2026 21:53. === Sayfa 435 ===
Accident : An occurrence associated with the operation of an aircraft which takes place between the time any person boards the aircraft with the intention of flight until such time as all persons have disembarked, in which: 1. A person is fatally or seriously injured as a result of: a. Being in the aircraft; b. Direct contact with any part of the aircraft, including parts which have become detached from the aircraft; or, c. Direct exposure to jet blast; except when the injuries are from natural causes, self-inflicted or inflicted by other persons, or when the injuries are to stowaways hiding outside the areas normally available to the passengers and crew: or 2. The aircraft sustains damage or structural failure which adversely affects the structural strength, performance or flight characteristics of the aircraft; and would normally require major repair or replacement of the affected component; except for engine failure or damage, when the damage is limited to the engine, its cowlings or accessories; or for damage limited to propellers, wing tips, antennas, tires, brakes, fairings, small dents or puncture holes in the aircraft skin: or 3. The aircraft is missing or is completely inaccessible.  Serious Injury:   A serious injury requires hospitalization for more than 48 hours within 7 days after the date of injury or any other reason like fracture of any bone, burns, damage to internal organs, infection or radiation (see ICAO Annex 13).  Dangerous Goods Incident:   An occurrence, other than a dangerous goods accident, associated with and related to the transport of dangerous goods, not necessarily occurring on board an aeroplane, which results in injury to a person, property damage, fire, breakage, spillage, leakage of fluid or radiation or other evidence that the integrity of the packaging has not been maintained. Any occurrence relating to the transport of dangerous goods which seriously jeopardizes the aeroplane or its occupants is also deemed to constitute a dangerous goods incident . Dangerous Goods Accident:   An occurrence associated with and related to the transport of dangerous goods which results in fatal or serious injury to a person or major property damage .  11.1.3 Handling Of The Post Serious Incident or Accident  In case of serious incident or accident flight crew shall follow the guidelines explained in LS.73.056 Post Incident/Accident Guide. This guide provides the flight crew instructions regarding handling the situation, notifying company and authorities and most importantly how to preserve the flight recorders data.  11.2 Occurrence Reporting 11.2.1 Crew Reporting Responsibilities  (A) The Commander is responsible for reporting all occurrences encountered while on duty via Safety Reporting System (SRS). A report filed by any other member of the crew does not relieve the Commander of this obligation. (B) Any crew member shall report to the Commander. 1. Any fault, failure, malfunction or defect which he believes may affect the airworthiness or safe operation of the aeroplane including emergency systems; 2. Any incident that endangered, or could have endangered the safety of the operation. The senior cabin crew member may co- ordinate the safety reporting from cabin crew to the Commander. 3. Any electronic interference suspected or identified by PEDs, description of the suspected device, the brand name and model number, its location in the aircraft at the time of the occurrence, interference symptoms, the device user’s contact details and the results of actions taken by the crew. (C) Regardless of rank, both pilots, who were at the controls of the airplane when the occurrence took place, shall submit individual air safety reports. In addition to operational report, Air Safety Report (ASR) shall be filled out for diverts which includes any flight safety issue. Otherwise, only operational report should be filled out. (D) All occurrences including “unlawful interference” shall be reported via SRS using Security Report (SEC). (E) For further analysis of a flight, Corporate Safety Department may request information from the crew of relevant flight. Such requests shall be fulfilled by submission of an ASR by flight crew on duty. 11.2.2. Commander Reporting Responsibilities  (A) Incident Reporting:  1. All flight crew on duty including Commander shall submit an ASR to Turkish Airlines of any incident that endangers or could endanger the safety of operation within 24 hours and Turkish Airlines shall forward the report to the Authority within 72 hours unless exceptional circumstances prevent this. If a report is not submitted within 48 hours, administrative penalties may be enforced by the Senior Vice President (Flight Operations)/Chief Pilot. 2. The Commander shall ensure that; a. passengers and crew are safe, b. the aircraft is secured, c. Flight recorders are deactivated and recordings are preserved (if necessary), d. Evidence regarding the incident is not lost, e. When necessary, Turkish government authority (if applicable) or local government authority is informed and help is requested. 3. The Commander shall ensure that all known or suspected technical defects and all exceedances of technical limitations occurring while he was responsible for the flight are recorded in the aircraft technical log. If the deficiency or exceedance of technical limitations endangers or could endanger the safety of operation, the Commander shall in addition initiate the submission of a report to the Turkish Airlines in accordance with item   (1)   above. 4. In the case of incidents reported in accordance with   Subchapter 11.2.1 and items ( 1 ) and ( 2 ) above, arising from, or relating to, any failure, malfunction or defect in the aeroplane, its equipment or any item of ground support equipment, or which cause or might cause   adverse   effects   on   the   continuing   airworthiness   of   the   aeroplane, Turkish Airlines   shall   also   inform   the   organization responsible for the design or the supplier or, if applicable, the organization responsible for continued airworthiness, at the same time as a report is submitted to the Authority. 5. The Commander shall notify the local authority without delay in the event of any emergency situation that necessitates an action in violation of local regulations and/or procedures. The commander shall also submit a report to the appropriate local authority and the Turkish Airlines if required by the state of occurrence. (B)   Accident and Serious Incident Reporting:  1. In case of an accident or serious incident that occurs in Turkish airspace, in the airspace of a foreign country whose sovereignty cannot be clarified or in international airspace, The Commander shall notify the local Authority and Turkish Airlines (Corporate Safety Directorate) by the quickest available means of any accidents or serious incidents resulting in injury, death or substantial aircraft damage occurring while he was responsible for the flight. In the event that the Commander is incapable of providing such notification, this task shall be undertaken by any other member of the crew if they are able to do so, note being taken of the succession of command specified in   Subchapter 4.3 or Corporate Safety Directorate by preparing the Accident/Incident Report which is included in the Attachment I of   DK.21.311 HKY-13 Regulation On Civil Air Vehicle Accidents or Serious Incidents  Investigation within 48 hours. 2. The Commander shall ensure that; a. passengers and crew are safe, b. the aircraft is secured, c. flight recorders are deactivated, recordings are preserved d. Evidence regarding the accident or serious incident is not lost, e. when necessary, Turkish government authority (if applicable) or local government authority is informed and help is requested. f. he gets an alcohol test immediately. g. he has the psychoactive substance test done if the government authority deems it necessary. 3. Turkish Airlines shall ensure that the Authority and any other organization required by the State to be informed, are notified by the quickest means available of any accident or serious incident and - in the case of accidents only - at least before the aeroplane is moved unless exceptional circumstances prevent this. I - Flight Procedures, and   DK.31.049 ICAO Doc 4444 | Procedures For Air Navigation Services - Air Traffic Management (PANS-ATM), State Regulations which give effect to these international standards, and the State Regulations themselves. Associated regulations are contained within Turkish DGCA and EASA Regulations. (B) An aircraft shall not be operated for the purpose of commercial air transportation other than in accordance with Turkish DGCA and EASA Regulations. All operations personnel shall be familiar and comply with the laws, regulations, standards and procedures of the States in which operations are conducted and with the contents of this manual relevant to the performance of their duties. (C) The Commander of an aircraft shall, whether manipulating the controls or not, be responsible for the operation of the aircraft in accordance with the rules of the air, except that the Commander may deviate from these rules in circumstances that render such departure absolutely necessary in the interests of safety. (D) Turkish Airlines, through its instructors, shall ensure that abnormal or emergency situations, requiring the application of part or all of abnormal or emergency procedures and simulation of IMC by artificial means are not simulated during commercial air transportation flights. (E) Turkish Airlines shall ensure that, in any kind of flights, with the purpose for seeking an approval for special authorization (ETOPS, LVO, etc.) in simulated conditions, flight crew of the intended flight will terminate the simulated flight conditions and revert back to original state in case of any emergency or abnormal situation and/or increase in cockpit workload related to flight safety is expected. (F) Turkish Airlines ensures that Air Traffic Services are used for all flights whenever available.  12.1.2 Information in Jeppesen  (A) The reference part of the   EK.10.73.002 Operations Manual Part-C Jeppesen Airway Manual contains relevant excerpts from the ICAO Documents. Distress: A condition of being threatened by serious and/or imminent danger and of requiring immediate assistance. 2. Urgency: A condition concerning the safety of an aircraft or other vehicle, or of some person on board or within sight, but does not require immediate assistance. (B) The pilot should start the emergency call with the appropriate international RTF prefix as follows: 1. Distress ‘MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY’ 2. Urgency ‘PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN’ (C) Pilots are urged – in their own interests – to request assistance from the ATC unit as soon as there is any doubt about the safe conduct of their flight. Even then, the provision of assistance may be delayed if a pilot does not pass clear details of his difficulties and requirements, using the international standard RTF prefix ‘MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY’ or ‘PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN’ as E K . 1 0 . 7 3 . 0 0 1 | R e v i s i o n 0 6 O p e r a t i o n s M a n u a l P a r t - A QMS Document Template Number: FR.18.0001 | Revision 12 Document Template Reference Document Number: TL.18.006 Page: 455 | Total Page: 466 Copy of this document has been generated on 9.01.2026 21:53. appropriate. For example, a vague request from a pilot for ‘confirmation of position’ is unlikely to be accorded as much priority as would be given to a statement that he is lost. If, subsequent to the transmission of a ‘MAYDAY’ or ‘PAN’, a pilot considers the problem not to be as serious as first thought and priority attention is no longer required, the emergency condition may be cancelled at the pilot’s discretion. It is invariably preferable for pilots believing themselves to be facing emergency situations to declare them as early as possible and then cancel later if they decide the situation allows. (D) If a pilot is already in communication with a civil or military ATC unit, before the emergency arises, assistance should be requested from the controller on the frequency in use. In this case, any SSR code setting previously assigned by ATC should be retained until instructions are received to change the code setting. (E) If, however, the pilot is not in direct communication with an ATC unit, the transponder should be switched, preferably before the emergency call is made, to Emergency Code 7700. If the transponding aircraft is high enough to be within secondary radar cover, the selection of the Emergency 7700 Code will alert the controller to the presence of an incident by means of an audio and visual warning. The received SSR plot will show the precise location of the aircraft on the controller’s radar display, and will then obviate the need for the controller to carry out the more time-consuming manual aircraft position plotting procedure. Standard Emergency and Urgency Transponder codes are: 7700 (Emergency), 7600 (Radio Failure) and 7500 (Unlawful Interference). Nature of the emergency; 6. Intention of the pilot-in-command; 7. Present or last known position, flight level/altitude and heading; 8. Any other useful information e.g. endurance remaining, number of people on board (POB), aircraft colour/markings, any survival aids. (H) An aircraft SSR transponder can also be used, during times of communication difficulties, by a pilot to acknowledge or respond to messages by the transmission of SSR Code changes or squawking 'Ident' as requested by the controller. (I) Any aeronautical station or aircraft knowing of an emergency incident may transmit a distress message whenever such action is necessary to obtain assistance for the aircraft in distress. In such circumstances, it should be made clear that the aircraft transmitting is not itself in distress. (J) Transmissions from aircraft in distress have priority over all other transmissions. On hearing a distress call, all stations must maintain radio silence on that frequency unless the distress is cancelled or the distress traffic is terminated; all distress traffic has been transferred to other frequencies; the station controlling communications gives permission; it has itself to render assistance. Any station which has knowledge of distress traffic, and which cannot itself assist the station in distress, shall nevertheless continue listening to such traffic until it is evident that assistance is being provided. Stations should take care not to interfere with the transmission of urgency calls. (K) The aircraft in distress or the station in control of a distress incident may impose silence either on all stations in the area or on any particular station that interferes with distress transmissions. The aeronautical station acknowledging a distress message on a particular frequency may consider it prudent to transfer other aircraft from that frequency in order to avoid any disruption of transmission from or to the emergency aircraft. (L) When an aircraft is no longer in distress it shall transmit a message cancelling the emergency condition. (M) When a distress incident has been resolved, the station which has been controlling the emergency traffic will transmit a message indicating that normal working may be resumed. (B) If the interference prevents satisfactory communication with your assigned ATC unit, request instructions using another listed frequency. LEASING  13.1 Leasing 13.1.1 General  (A) Leasing, within this chapter, is understood to be a contractual arrangement between Turkish Airlines and another operator of an aeroplane, to lease in or lease out aeroplanes. It is mainly differentiated in two cases: 1. the lessor and/or lessee is Turkish Operator, 2. the lessor and/or lessee is non-Turkish operator. (B) In order to maintain a high level of safety and to avoid large variations of maintenance and/or operational standards, larger requirements are imposed in case (2). (C) For detailed Company process related to leasing, see   PR.10.19.014 Procedure for Wet Lease In Operations (D)   DK.22.065 SHT-KİRALAMA | Instruction On The Procedures and Principles For Aircraft Leasing procedures will be applied for leasing operations. (E)   In   wet   lease   and   short-term   wet-lease   operations,   the   continuous   airworthiness,   flight   operation   and   other   administrative responsibilities of the flight activities carried out during the lease period belong to the company leasing the aircraft, while the commercial responsibility belongs to the lessee. These issues must be clearly stated in the lease agreement. (F) For aircraft financially leased from the non-Turkish company and registered in the Turkish Civil Aircraft Registry to be leased to another company, the financial leasing agreements must state that the aircraft owner has given permission for the lease. If there is no statement regarding this issue in the financial leasing agreements, a permission letter must be obtained from the aircraft owner. Wet-Lease : A leasing agreement between operators, for an aeroplane with its crew where the aeroplane is operated under the AOC of the lessor and under the commercial control of the lessee, using the lessee's airline designator code and traffic rights.  Short Term Wet-Lease : Wet Lease Contract lasting no more than 72 hours.  Wet-Lease In : Leasing any aircraft for the fleet of the Company from any other airline company for a temporary period.  Wet-Lease Out : Agreement executed in case of leasing out the aircraft registered to the Company to another airline company.  Lessee : A commercial air transportation company that acquires the use of an aircraft for a specified period in return for a fee under a lease agreement.  Lessor : A commercial air transport company that gives an aircraft to another commercial air transport company for a certain period of time in return for a fee.  13.1.3 Leasing of Aeroplanes Between Turkish Airlines and Turkish Operators 13.1.3.1 Dry Lease Between Turkish Airlines and Turkish Operators  It is not applicable that the Turkish DGCA does not have any procedure for Dry-Lease In and Dry-Lease Out process between Turkish Operators.  13.1.3.2 Wet-Lease Between Turkish Airlines and Turkish Operators  In accordance with   DK.22.065 SHT-KİRALAMA | Instruction On The Procedures and Principles For Aircraft Leasing issued by the Turkish DGCA, there is no pre-approval process for the agreement between Turkish Operators. Wet-Lease In application are carried out on condition that an application is made to the Turkish DGCA at least 15 days before the start date of the operation and approval is received in a manner that meets the requirements in Annex 6 of   DK.22.065 SHT-KİRALAMA |  Instruction On The Procedures and Principles For Aircraft Leasing.
